lessons.title: Regional Instability After the Iran-Iraq War

before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark narrative account on this topic, examiners want a chain of cause and consequence, not a list of dates. Pick three linked moments — for example, the 1988 ceasefire leaving Iraq with $80bn debt, Saddam’s 1989 demands that Kuwait write off the loans, and the 1990 OPEC dispute — and use connectives such as ‘this meant that’ and ‘as a result’ to show how each step pushed the region towards war. Use specialist vocabulary (reparations, Ba’athism, Tanker War) to lift your SPaG band.

practice_questions.text: Write a narrative account analysing how the consequences of the Iran-Iraq war created tensions in the Gulf between 1988 and 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Iraq emerged from the 1980–88 war with around $80 billion of debt, including roughly $14–15 billion owed to Kuwait, creating direct financial pressure on Saddam Hussein's regime.
• Saddam expected Gulf states to write off loans as reparations for defending the Arab world from Iran's revolution; their refusal — particularly Kuwait's — sharpened his grievance.
• A million-man army could not be demobilised without political risk, so Iraq remained on a war footing in peacetime, encouraging external solutions to internal problems.
• Saddam's 1989–90 demand that OPEC raise oil prices to ease his debt clashed with Kuwait's overproduction, turning a debt dispute into an oil-price dispute.
• Use of chemical weapons at Halabja in 1988 had drawn only muted Western criticism, so Saddam believed brutal action carried little international cost.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Iraqi regime in the aftermath of the Iran-Iraq war.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A cult of personality around Saddam Hussein, with state media presenting him as the indispensable defender of the Arab world against the Iranian revolution.
• A million-strong army that the regime could not afford to demobilise, leaving Iraq on a permanent war footing despite the 1988 ceasefire.
• Continued use of brutal repression, including the chemical weapons attack on Kurdish civilians at Halabja in March 1988.
• Domination of military and intelligence posts by Saddam's clan from Tikrit, tightening Ba'athist control after the war.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 1 for development with specific detail.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Tanker War (1984–88) for the wider Gulf region.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Tanker War showed how easily Gulf oil shipping could be disrupted, drawing US and Western navies into the region as escorts and rehearsing the kind of intervention later seen in 1990–91.
• It frightened global insurance markets and crashed Iraqi oil revenues, deepening the debt crisis Saddam could not escape after 1988.
• It taught Saddam that targeting tankers brought economic costs but limited international punishment — a lesson he carried into his treatment of Kuwait's oil exports.
• It exposed the strategic vulnerability of the Strait of Hormuz, hardening Western determination to keep the Gulf open by force if needed.
[8 marks — Mastering: Significance evaluated at the time and over the period leading to 1990, with concrete detail. Secure: Two clear significances with development. Developing: One developed and one undeveloped point. Emerging: Description of the Tanker War with little reference to significance.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Iraq's situation in 1989 was similar to or different from its situation in 1980.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Different — in 1980 Iraq launched the war with a healthy oil-funded economy; in 1989 it carried roughly $80 billion of war debt that crippled reconstruction.
• Similar — in both years Saddam led a Ba'athist regime built on a cult of personality, with the security services dominant and dissent crushed.
• Different — in 1980 Saddam had relatively limited combat experience; by 1989 he commanded a million-man, battle-hardened army equipped with chemical weapons.
• Similar — in both years Iraq's relationship with Kuwait was strained by border and oil-field disputes around Rumaila.
[4 marks — 2 marks per way: 1 for identification, 1 for development with specific contrast.]

practice_questions.text: Explain a development in Iraqi foreign policy between the 1988 ceasefire and the summer of 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A shift from diplomacy with the Gulf monarchies to public confrontation, as Saddam moved from asking for debt write-offs to publicly accusing Kuwait of economic warfare.
• Increasing pressure on OPEC for higher oil prices, framing Kuwait's overproduction as deliberate sabotage of Iraq's recovery.
• Sharper rhetoric of pan-Arab leadership, casting Iraq as the defender of the Arab nation entitled to financial support from richer neighbours.
• Growing use of military threats over the Rumaila oil field and Kuwaiti islands, foreshadowing the August 1990 invasion.
[8 marks — Mastering: Coherent account of change over the period with specific developments dated. Secure: Two clear developments with some detail. Developing: One developed point. Emerging: Generalised account without dated developments.]

practice_questions.text: Compare two interpretations of why the Iran-Iraq war ended without resolving regional tensions. (Suggest two contrasting historical views.)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• One interpretation emphasises economic causes — Iraq's $80 billion debt and collapsed oil revenue meant peace simply paused the war and reset the conditions for the next conflict.
• A contrasting interpretation emphasises regime ideology — Saddam's Ba'athist cult of personality and cult of military strength meant a leader who could not climb down without an external victory.
• A third view stresses unfinished disputes — the Shatt al-Arab waterway, Halabja and the Kurdish question were all left legally unresolved by Resolution 598.
• Both interpretations agree the 1988 ceasefire was a pause, not a settlement.
[4 marks — 2 marks per interpretation identified and supported with specific evidence.]

lessons.title: Western, Russian and Regional Interests in the Gulf

before.content_html:
A Region the World Could Not Ignore

In 1990 the Persian Gulf produced roughly a quarter of the world’s oil and held around two-thirds of its proven reserves. Every barrel exported by sea had to pass through one narrow choke point: the Strait of Hormuz, just thirty-three kilometres wide at its narrowest. Whoever could threaten Hormuz could threaten the global economy. That single geographical fact shaped how Washington, Moscow, London and Tel Aviv thought about the Gulf, and why an Iraqi invasion of Kuwait would never be treated as a private quarrel between Arab neighbours.

Oil was not the only reason outsiders were involved. The Cold War, the Iranian Revolution and the unresolved Israeli-Palestinian conflict all converged on the Gulf, each pulling rival powers towards different local clients. By 1990 these threads had braided into a regional order that was visibly unstable — one in which Saddam Hussein could plausibly read different signals from different capitals at the same time.

Key Fact

By 1990 the Gulf held roughly two-thirds of the world’s proven oil reserves, and around a fifth of that oil moved by sea through the Strait of Hormuz. The 1979 Iranian Revolution had already shown how violently regional change could shock the global economy.

Cold War Patterns and the 1979 Reset

For most of the Cold War the United States had backed the Shah of Iran as its anchor in the Gulf, while the Soviet Union signed friendship treaties and arms deals with Iraq. The 1979 revolution shattered the pattern: Iran turned hostile to Washington overnight, US embassy staff were taken hostage in Tehran, and within months the USSR invaded neighbouring Afghanistan. Both superpowers were suddenly without a comfortable client in the region.

Through the 1980s, the United States quietly tilted towards Iraq during the Iran-Iraq war, sharing satellite intelligence and removing Iraq from its list of state sponsors of terrorism in 1982. This was realpolitik: Washington did not approve of Saddam, but it preferred a strong Iraq to a victorious Khomeini. The Soviets continued to sell weapons to Iraq, while also opening cautious channels to Iran. By 1989, with the Berlin Wall down and Mikhail Gorbachev seeking better relations with Washington, the rules of the game were visibly changing — but old alignments and old client relationships had not.

OPEC tried to manage the world oil price by setting member quotas. Each barrel above quota meant a lower price; each barrel below meant a higher one. In 1989–90 Saddam wanted prices high so he could pay his $80 billion war debt. Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates kept producing above quota, pushing prices down. Saddam estimated that every $1 fall in the oil price cost Iraq about $1 billion a year in revenue. To him, Kuwaiti overproduction was not just business — it was, in his rhetoric, an act of economic war on a country that had bled defending its neighbours.

The Israeli-Palestinian Conflict as Recruitment Tool

Tensions in the Gulf could not be cleanly separated from the older quarrel further west. The First Intifada, which broke out in December 1987, dominated Arab television screens just as Iraqi soldiers were coming home from the Iran front. Images of Israeli soldiers confronting stone-throwing Palestinian teenagers played nightly across the region, and US support for Israel was a fixture in every public-opinion poll from Cairo to Karachi.

For aspiring jihadist movements, this was a recruitment opportunity. Veterans returning from the Soviet-Afghan war found audiences willing to believe that the United States was the patron of every Arab grievance — the dispossession of Palestinians, the propping up of monarchies, the bases on Saudi soil. The Israeli-Palestinian conflict did not cause the 1990 Gulf crisis, but it gave Saddam useful pan-Arab cover (he later tried to link any Iraqi withdrawal from Kuwait to Israeli withdrawal from the West Bank), and it helped shape the worldview that produced al-Qaeda later in the decade.

Why the Outside Powers Could Not Stay Out

By 1990 the Gulf had a settled pattern of outside involvement. The United States kept a small naval presence and close ties with Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the smaller Gulf states — many of which hosted American advisers and bought American weapons. Britain, France and other European powers maintained commercial and arms links. The Soviet Union still saw Iraq as a long-standing client, although Gorbachev was now willing to coordinate with Washington at the UN. Iran was isolated and rebuilding. Israel watched warily, fearing that any large Arab army — especially one armed with chemical weapons and Scud missiles — could be turned westward.

This is the world Saddam was trying to read in the summer of 1990. He saw a superpower (the USA) preoccupied with Eastern Europe, a rival superpower (the USSR) in retreat from Afghanistan, and Arab neighbours he believed owed him gratitude. He underestimated how completely a serious threat to Gulf oil supplies would unite outside powers across that whole spectrum.

It is tempting to imagine that with the Berlin Wall down, the superpower contest evaporated. In the Gulf it lingered. The USSR’s arms-export relationships with Iraq did not end overnight. American basing arrangements with Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Kuwait pre-dated 1989 and outlived 1991. Old patterns of Western and Russian interests — oil security, arms markets, regional influence — survived the end of European communism intact. The 1991 Gulf War was the first major crisis of the post-Cold War order, but its players were still using Cold War muscle memory.

Key Fact

Outside involvement in the Gulf was driven by three overlapping interests — oil supply (Strait of Hormuz, OPEC), Cold War alignments (Soviet-Iraqi arms ties, US-Saudi defence links), and the pull of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. None of these disappeared in 1989, and all of them shaped responses to the 1990 invasion.
before.exam_tip_html: For a 12-mark source-utility question, examiners want all three of content (what the source actually says), provenance (who, when, why) and your own knowledge weighed together — not two of the three. A 1990 US State Department briefing is useful for showing official Western thinking but limited because it could not yet know how the crisis would end. A 2016 Chilcot reflection has hindsight but reflects later political pressures. Always set your source in its proper political context using the realpolitik, OPEC and First Intifada vocabulary from this lesson to lift your SPaG band.

practice_questions.text: Source A is an extract from a 1990 US State Department internal briefing on Gulf oil security. Source B is an extract from a 2016 retrospective in a UK foreign-affairs journal looking back on Western interests in the Gulf in 1990. Study the two sources. How useful are they for understanding why outside powers were drawn into the Gulf in 1990?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Source A is contemporary, written by officials with direct access to oil-supply intelligence — useful for showing official Western priorities at the time, especially the Strait of Hormuz and OPEC dynamics. Limited because it cannot reflect on outcomes and is shaped by realpolitik framing.
• Source B has the benefit of hindsight, drawing on declassified material and post-Chilcot reflection — useful for weighing whether 1990 priorities were proportionate, but coloured by later political controversies.
• Own knowledge: Gulf held two-thirds of proven oil reserves; Strait of Hormuz carried roughly a fifth of seaborne oil; OPEC quota disputes and the First Intifada reinforced perceptions of US bias.
• A judgement should weigh the two sources rather than dismissing one as biased — both have value if their provenance is read carefully.
[12 marks — Mastering: Integrated content, provenance and own knowledge with substantiated overall judgement on usefulness. Secure: Clear use of all three with some judgement. Developing: Two of the three integrated. Emerging: Surface-level reference to who wrote each source.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of US policy in the Gulf during the late 1980s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A tilt towards Iraq during the Iran-Iraq war as a counterweight to revolutionary Iran, including sharing satellite intelligence and removing Iraq from the state-sponsors-of-terrorism list in 1982.
• A network of basing and arms-supply agreements with Gulf monarchies — particularly Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Bahrain — protecting access to oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
• Tolerance of brutal Iraqi behaviour such as the Halabja chemical attack in 1988, framed as the price of containing Iran.
• Naval re-flagging of Kuwaiti tankers during the Tanker War to keep oil exports moving under US protection.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 1 for development with specific detail.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Strait of Hormuz for international involvement in the Gulf.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Around a fifth of seaborne global oil passed through Hormuz, so any threat to it had immediate implications for the world economy and locked outside powers into Gulf security.
• The Tanker War of 1984–88 had already shown how easily shipping in and around Hormuz could be disrupted, drawing US and Western navies into permanent re-flagging and escort missions.
• Its narrowness (around 33 km) made it a credible point of leverage for any state hostile to Western interests, raising the stakes of any conflict in the Gulf.
• Significance over time: Hormuz remained a strategic priority through the 1991 war, the 2003 invasion and beyond, embedding the US navy in the region.
[8 marks — Mastering: Significance evaluated at the time and over the period with concrete detail. Secure: Two clear significances with development. Developing: One developed and one undeveloped point. Emerging: Description of the strait with limited reference to significance.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Soviet and American interests in the Gulf were similar in the late 1980s.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Similar — both wanted a stable supply of Gulf oil to global markets, since price shocks affected their economies and those of their allies.
• Similar — both feared a regional war that could spiral into superpower confrontation, encouraging cautious arms transfers and crisis management at the UN.
• Similar — both maintained client relationships in the region (USSR with Iraq, USA with Saudi Arabia and the smaller Gulf states), even as the Cold War wound down in Europe.
• Similar — both watched Iran with suspicion after 1979, although for different ideological reasons.
[4 marks — 2 marks per similarity: 1 for identification, 1 for development with specific evidence.]

practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:

• Saddam Hussein began linking Iraqi grievances to the Palestinian cause, casting himself as the leader of an Arab nation betrayed by the West.
• Returning Arab veterans from the Soviet-Afghan war absorbed Intifada imagery, helping to shape the jihadist narrative that the United States was the patron of every Arab grievance.
• In August 1990 Saddam tried to make an Iraqi withdrawal from Kuwait conditional on Israeli withdrawal from the West Bank, an explicit attempt to link the two conflicts.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: Explain a development in the relationship between the United States and Iraq between 1980 and 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A shift in the early 1980s from neutrality to a tilt towards Iraq during the Iran-Iraq war, including intelligence sharing and removal from the terrorism list in 1982.
• Tolerance through the mid-1980s of Iraqi chemical weapons use as the price of containing Iran, even after the Halabja attack of 1988.
• Growing unease in 1989–90 as Saddam's rhetoric turned against Kuwait, with US officials sending mixed signals about whether border disputes were America's concern.
• A sharp break in August 1990 when the invasion of Kuwait turned a tilted partner into a strategic enemy almost overnight.
[8 marks — Mastering: Coherent account of change over the period with specific developments dated. Secure: Two clear developments with some detail. Developing: One developed point. Emerging: Generalised account without dated developments.]

before.content_html:
A Crisis Looking for a Pretext

By the spring of 1990, Saddam Hussein had a list of grievances against Kuwait long enough to fit any rhetoric he chose. Iraq owed Kuwait around $14–15 billion. Kuwait was producing oil above its OPEC quota and pushing prices down. Iraq had a long-running border claim to two Kuwaiti islands, Bubiyan and Warbah, which would give Iraqi ports better access to the Gulf. And Saddam alleged that Kuwait was practising slant-drilling at the Rumaila oil field, stealing crude from beneath Iraqi soil.

Whether or not the slant-drilling claim was technically true, it became the public face of the crisis. In a July 1990 speech Saddam called Kuwaiti and Emirati overproduction “a kind of war against Iraq”, and warned that Iraq would not accept death by slow economic strangulation. The grievances were real; what is harder to know is whether Saddam genuinely believed Kuwait was robbing him, or whether he was assembling a justification for an invasion he had already decided to launch.

Key Fact

Saddam’s public case for action against Kuwait rested on four grievances — unpaid war debts, Kuwaiti oil overproduction, a long-running border dispute over Bubiyan and Warbah islands, and accusations of slant-drilling at the Rumaila oil field.

The Jeddah Talks and the Glaspie Meeting

In late July 1990 Saudi mediation produced a last-ditch negotiation in Jeddah between Iraqi and Kuwaiti officials. Iraq demanded debt forgiveness, $2.4 billion in compensation for Rumaila, the lease of Bubiyan and Warbah islands, and a binding agreement on oil quotas. Kuwait offered some financial easing but refused the territorial demands. The talks broke down on 1 August 1990; the next day Iraqi tanks crossed the border.

Days before the invasion, on 25 July, Saddam met the US ambassador April Glaspie in Baghdad. Glaspie said the United States had “no opinion on Arab-Arab conflicts, like your border disagreement with Kuwait”. Critics later argued that the line gave Saddam a green light. Glaspie’s defenders countered that she also warned against the use of force, and that Saddam was always going to read what he wanted to read. Either way, Saddam appears to have come away believing the United States would not fight to defend Kuwait.

Internal Iraqi planning had originally focused on a limited operation: seize Bubiyan and Warbah, occupy the Rumaila field, and force a humiliated Kuwait to renegotiate. By the time orders were issued, the plan had grown. The annexation announcement on 8 August declared Kuwait the “19th province” of Iraq, with Iraqi flags raised over Kuwait City and Iraqi licence plates issued for civilian cars. The shift from coercion to annexation was Saddam’s critical miscalculation: a limited grab might have provoked condemnation but not war, full annexation forced every other state to choose a side.

The Invasion, 2 August 1990

Iraqi forces crossed the Kuwaiti border at around 2am local time on 2 August 1990. The spearhead was the Republican Guard, supported by helicopter-borne special forces who seized Kuwait City’s government buildings, the airport and the Dasman Palace before sunrise. Kuwait’s military, around 16,000 strong, was outnumbered roughly six to one and was not on full alert. By the end of the first day, organised resistance had effectively collapsed.

The al-Sabah dynasty — Emir Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah and his family — fled to Saudi Arabia in the early hours, taking the country’s sovereign-wealth records with them. Iraqi troops looted gold reserves, art collections and supermarket shelves. Within a week Iraq announced an interim government in Kuwait City led by an Iraqi-appointed officer; on 8 August it formally annexed the country. Saddam now had a fait accompli: occupying Kuwait was already a done deed, and reversing it would require force.

A Miscalculation, Not a Masterstroke

From inside Baghdad the invasion looked logical. It cancelled the debts (because Kuwait no longer existed as a separate state). It seized Kuwait’s vast oil reserves, doubling Iraq’s share of world reserves at a stroke. It would intimidate the rest of the Gulf into deference. And it offered the spectacle of a pan-Arab leader correcting an old colonial border, repackaging a financial crisis as a nationalist triumph.

From outside Baghdad it looked very different. Saudi Arabia now feared its eastern oil fields were next. The United States saw a state seizing twenty per cent of the world’s oil reserves. Even the Soviet Union, Iraq’s old patron, was not willing to defend an outright annexation at the United Nations. Within hours the UN Security Council passed Resolution 660 condemning the invasion. Within days, the US and the UK had begun deploying forces to Saudi Arabia. Saddam’s gamble had not silenced his enemies; it had unified them.

It is a recurring claim that the US ambassador April Glaspie green-lit the invasion in her 25 July meeting. The transcript shows a more complicated picture: Glaspie repeated standard diplomatic language about not taking sides in Arab-Arab disputes, but she also said the United States expected disagreements to be resolved peacefully. The deeper point is that Saddam was looking for evidence to support a decision he was already making. Treating Glaspie as the cause of the invasion underplays Saddam’s own agency — the cash crisis, the Rumaila claim and the army he could not afford to demobilise are the real drivers.

Key Fact

The invasion of Kuwait was launched at 2am on 2 August 1990 and Kuwait City fell within hours. By 8 August Iraq had annexed Kuwait as its “19th province”. The short-term gain was huge — doubled oil reserves, cancelled debts — but the move united outside powers against Iraq almost overnight.
before.exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark source-analysis question on Saddam’s motives, examiners want you to read the source carefully (what does it actually claim?) and then make two clear inferences supported by short, embedded quotation. A July 1990 speech by Saddam might suggest economic motives (Kuwaiti overproduction as ‘a kind of war against Iraq’) and pan-Arab justification (defending the Arab nation). Avoid the common error of judging a source biased and stopping there — even openly biased sources tell us what their author wanted their audience to believe.

practice_questions.text: Source A is an extract from a televised speech by Saddam Hussein, 17 July 1990, addressing the Iraqi people on Kuwaiti oil overproduction. Study the source. What does it suggest about Saddam's reasons for invading Kuwait?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The source suggests economic motives — Saddam frames Kuwaiti overproduction as deliberate harm to the Iraqi economy and uses the language of 'war' to justify his response.
• It also suggests pan-Arab framing — Saddam presents Iraq as defender of the Arab nation, casting himself as an injured leader seeking justice rather than territory.
• A quotation showing the rhetorical pivot from grievance to threat (e.g. 'a kind of war against Iraq') would support the inference.
• Limited utility on its own: as a public speech, it tells us what Saddam wanted the audience to believe, not necessarily the full internal calculation.
[4 marks — 2 marks per inference clearly supported by reference to the source.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait on 2 August 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Spearheaded by the Republican Guard, supported by helicopter-borne special forces who seized Kuwait City government buildings, the airport and Dasman Palace before sunrise.
• A six-to-one numerical advantage that overwhelmed Kuwait's roughly 16,000-strong military within hours.
• Followed within a week by formal annexation, with Kuwait declared Iraq's '19th province' on 8 August 1990.
• Looting of Kuwaiti gold reserves, sovereign assets and civilian supplies during the occupation.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 1 for development with specific detail.]

practice_questions.text: Write a narrative account analysing the events between the breakdown of the Jeddah talks and the annexation of Kuwait.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Jeddah talks broke down on 1 August 1990 when Kuwait refused Iraq's territorial and financial demands.
• Iraqi forces crossed the border at around 2am on 2 August, with the Republican Guard taking Kuwait City within hours; the al-Sabah dynasty fled to Saudi Arabia.
• The UN Security Council passed Resolution 660 within hours, condemning the invasion and demanding withdrawal.
• On 8 August Iraq announced the formal annexation of Kuwait as its '19th province', escalating the crisis from coercion to outright land grab.
• The annexation hardened international opinion, made a negotiated reversal almost impossible, and brought US and UK forces to Saudi Arabia.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Rumaila oil field dispute in the build-up to the 1990 invasion.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Rumaila gave Saddam a concrete, public-facing grievance — slant-drilling allegations turned an abstract debt dispute into a charge of theft from Iraqi soil.
• The $2.4 billion Iraqi compensation demand at Jeddah came directly out of the Rumaila claim, defining the negotiating space and contributing to the breakdown of talks.
• Significance over time: control of Rumaila and access to the Gulf via Bubiyan and Warbah remained Iraqi strategic objectives that long outlived the 1991 ceasefire.
• It illustrated how regional border arrangements left over from the colonial era could be weaponised by ambitious states.
[8 marks — Mastering: Significance evaluated at the time and over the period with concrete detail. Secure: Two clear significances with development. Developing: One developed and one undeveloped point. Emerging: Description of Rumaila with limited reference to significance.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Saddam's grievances against Kuwait were similar to or different from his grievances against the Gulf monarchies in general.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Similar — both rested on the claim that wealthy Gulf states owed Iraq financial support for the Iran-Iraq war, framed as reparations.
• Different — Kuwait carried specific border and oil-field disputes (Bubiyan, Warbah, Rumaila) that did not apply to Saudi Arabia or the UAE.
• Similar — Saddam used pan-Arab rhetoric against all the Gulf monarchies, presenting them as betraying the Arab nation by hosting Western forces or producing too much oil.
• Different — only Kuwait was annexed and absorbed as a 'province'; the other Gulf states were threatened, not invaded.
[4 marks — 2 marks per way: 1 for identification, 1 for development with specific contrast.]

practice_questions.text: Explain a development in the international response to events in the Gulf in the first week of August 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A rapid UN Security Council response: Resolution 660 condemned the invasion within hours, followed by Resolution 661 imposing sanctions.
• A coordinated US-UK military response, with President Bush ordering US forces to Saudi Arabia at King Fahd's invitation, and Margaret Thatcher backing immediate action.
• A surprising Soviet alignment with Washington at the UN, signalling that Cold War-era cover for Iraq had ended.

lessons.title: Bush, Thatcher and Building the Coalition

before.content_html:
The First Phone Calls

When Iraqi tanks rolled into Kuwait City in the early hours of 2 August 1990, President George H. W. Bush was at his Maine summer house in Kennebunkport. Margaret Thatcher was in Aspen, Colorado, attending a conference. Within hours both leaders had spoken; within a day they were sitting together at the Aspen Institute. The image of the two of them — Bush cautious, Thatcher already certain — would shape the diplomacy of the next six months.

Thatcher’s line at Aspen, “remember George, this is no time to go wobbly”, captured Britain’s position. The annexation of Kuwait was, in her view, an unambiguous breach of international law that had to be reversed by force if necessary. Bush, more cautious by temperament, agreed within days. By 5 August he was telling reporters at Andrews Air Force Base, “this will not stand, this aggression against Kuwait”. The choice had been made: Kuwait would be liberated, not negotiated.

Key Fact

Two UN resolutions framed the international response. UN Resolution 660 on 2 August demanded immediate Iraqi withdrawal. UN Resolution 678 on 29 November set the deadline of 15 January 1991, after which member states could use “all necessary means”.

Operation Desert Shield

The first military priority was not liberating Kuwait but defending Saudi Arabia. Iraqi armoured divisions sat on the Saudi border, and the Saudi eastern oil fields were unprotected. King Fahd had to choose between trusting the United States to send forces or watching Saddam set the agenda for the whole region. After tense diplomacy — Defense Secretary Dick Cheney flew to Riyadh to brief the Saudi cabinet — King Fahd issued a formal invitation on 7 August 1990.

Operation Desert Shield moved the largest American military force overseas since Vietnam. By autumn around 250,000 US troops were in the Gulf; by December the total coalition force exceeded 500,000. Britain’s contribution, codenamed Operation Granby, eventually included some 53,000 personnel including the 1st Armoured Division.

Bush and his Secretary of State James Baker insisted that the coalition had to be visibly Arab as well as Western. If the operation looked like a colonial war by Christian powers against a Muslim country, Saddam’s pan-Arab framing would gain traction. The price of Arab cover was relentless coalition diplomacy. Egypt sent two divisions, Syria sent one (a remarkable diplomatic moment given Hafez al-Assad’s usual hostility to Washington), and Saudi Arabia provided forces as well as bases. Crucially, Israel was kept out of the coalition entirely — bringing Israel in would have driven the Arab states straight back out.

The UN Campaign

Bush ran the diplomatic campaign through the United Nations rather than around it. Resolution 660 condemned the invasion within hours of the first reports. Resolution 661, four days later, imposed comprehensive economic sanctions. Through autumn 1990 a stream of further resolutions tightened the noose: blockading Iraqi shipping, banning air travel, demanding the release of foreign hostages Saddam was using as “human shields”.

Resolution 678 was the decisive step. Passed on 29 November 1990 by twelve votes to two (Cuba and Yemen) with one abstention (China), it authorised member states to use “all necessary means” to enforce the previous resolutions if Iraq had not withdrawn by 15 January 1991. The phrase “all necessary means” was the diplomatic permission for war — without it, military action would have lacked legitimacy and Arab support would have crumbled.

Funding and the Strange New World Order

Wars are expensive. The 1990–91 deployment cost roughly $61 billion in 1991 dollars, and the United States insisted that allies who benefited should pay. Saudi Arabia and Kuwait-in-exile each contributed around $16 billion. Germany and Japan, both forbidden by their constitutions from sending combat troops, contributed roughly $10 billion and $13 billion respectively. The result was a war the United States led but did not pay for — a model that would not be repeated.

The Soviet Union’s position was a quiet revolution. Mikhail Gorbachev refused to veto the UN resolutions, even though Iraq had been a Soviet client. Soviet diplomats pressed Saddam to withdraw, while keeping channels open in case a last-minute deal could be reached. For Bush, this was the “new world order” he spoke of in a September 1990 address to Congress — a post-Cold War system in which the great powers would cooperate against aggression. For Saddam, it was the most unwelcome surprise of the crisis.

Students often picture a US-UK operation with a few foreign flags pinned on for show. The reality was 35 contributing nations — including, importantly, Egypt, Syria, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Morocco. The Arab and Muslim share of the ground force was a deliberate diplomatic achievement. Soviet acquiescence at the UN, although not active participation, denied Saddam the cover of superpower rivalry. Without that wide coalition the operation would not have happened, or would have collapsed politically before it could begin.

Key Fact

By January 1991 a 35-nation coalition with around 700,000 troops sat in Saudi Arabia, paid for largely by allies, with Soviet acquiescence at the UN and a Resolution 678 deadline counting down. Saddam had assumed the world was too divided to act; in fact it had assembled in front of him.
before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark narrative account on the international response, examiners want to see causation, not chronology. Trace at least three linked steps — for example, the immediate US-UK alignment at Aspen, the deployment to Saudi Arabia under King Fahd’s invitation, and the November vote on Resolution 678 — and use connectives such as ‘this enabled’, ‘as a result’ and ‘in turn’. Specialist vocabulary (sanctions, coalition diplomacy, no-fly zone) is required at the top band.

practice_questions.text: Write a narrative account analysing how the international community responded to the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait between August and November 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• On 2 August UN Security Council Resolution 660 condemned the invasion and demanded immediate withdrawal; Resolution 661 followed with comprehensive sanctions on 6 August.
• Bush and Thatcher aligned at Aspen on 2 August, with Thatcher's 'don't go wobbly' insistence shaping the firm allied response.
• King Fahd invited US forces to Saudi Arabia on 7 August, beginning Operation Desert Shield and the largest American overseas deployment since Vietnam.
• A 35-nation coalition was assembled through autumn 1990, with Egyptian, Syrian and Saudi divisions providing crucial Arab cover; Germany and Japan contributed funding.
• On 29 November Resolution 678 authorised 'all necessary means' if Iraq had not withdrawn by 15 January 1991, supplying the legal basis for war.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Operation Desert Shield.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A defensive deployment to Saudi Arabia from August 1990 at King Fahd's invitation, designed to deter further Iraqi advance into the eastern oil fields.
• The largest American overseas troop deployment since Vietnam, reaching around 250,000 US personnel by autumn 1990 and around 700,000 coalition troops by January.
• A 35-nation coalition, including Egyptian, Syrian and Saudi divisions, providing visible Arab cover for the operation.
• Substantial financial contributions from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait-in-exile, Germany and Japan covering most of the deployment cost.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 1 for development with specific detail.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of UN Resolution 678 for the conduct of the 1991 Gulf War.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Resolution 678 supplied the legal authorisation for military action — without it, the use of force would have lacked international legitimacy and Arab support would likely have collapsed.
• It set the 15 January 1991 deadline, transforming an open-ended diplomatic standoff into a countdown that pressured both Iraq and the coalition.
• It signalled Soviet acquiescence at the UN, removing the prospect of superpower deadlock and showing the post-Cold War order Bush was talking about could function in practice.
• Significance over time: the 'all necessary means' formula became the template for later UN authorisations (e.g. Libya 2011), with both supporters and critics referring back to 678.
[8 marks — Mastering: Significance evaluated at the time and over the period with concrete detail. Secure: Two clear significances with development. Developing: One developed and one undeveloped point. Emerging: Description of the resolution with limited reference to significance.]

practice_questions.text: Source A is the official US Joint Chiefs of Staff briefing to Congress on Operation Desert Shield, October 1990. Study the source. Evaluate the usefulness of this source to a historian investigating the build-up to the 1991 war. (You may use any other relevant evidence in your evaluation.)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Content: a briefing of this kind sets out US war planning, troop numbers, allied contributions and operational assumptions — useful for understanding what the Pentagon thought was achievable.
• Provenance: the Joint Chiefs are insiders, so the source is well-informed; but they are also seeking funding and political support, which can shape what they emphasise.
• Own knowledge: by October 1990 around 250,000 US troops were in theatre under Operation Desert Shield, with King Fahd's August invitation and the November Resolution 678 vote still ahead.
• Limitations: contemporary military briefings tend to omit political doubts and downplay risks — useful for the planning picture, less useful for diplomatic context.
• Judgement: the source is genuinely useful provided it is read alongside diplomatic evidence such as UN resolutions and contemporary press coverage, not in isolation.
[12 marks — Mastering: Integrated content, provenance and own knowledge with substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Clear use of all three with some judgement. Developing: Two of the three integrated. Emerging: Surface-level reference to who wrote the source.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Bush's and Thatcher's responses to the invasion were similar.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Similar — both rejected any negotiated outcome that left Kuwait under Iraqi control, framing the annexation as an unacceptable breach of international law.
• Similar — both worked through the UN Security Council, treating multilateral authorisation as essential to political legitimacy.
• Similar — both committed substantial national forces to the coalition (Operation Desert Shield and Operation Granby) and invested political capital in the operation.
• Different in tone but not direction — Bush was more cautious early on, Thatcher more decisive (the 'don't go wobbly' line), but they reached the same operational conclusions within days.
[4 marks — 2 marks per similarity: 1 for identification, 1 for development with specific evidence.]

practice_questions.text: Compare two interpretations of why Margaret Thatcher's role at Aspen was important. Explain why these interpretations differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretations differ because authors emphasise different evidence: Thatcher's own memoirs stress her steel and influence over a wavering Bush; American memoirs of the period give more credit to Bush's own team and treat Thatcher as one voice among several.
• They differ in purpose: a British political memoir is shaping a legacy, while a US National Security Council account is allocating credit within Washington.
• They differ in timing of writing: post-1990 reflections written immediately tend to dramatise Thatcher's role; later, calmer accounts after declassification show a more collaborative process.
• Both interpretations agree the Aspen meeting mattered, even if they disagree on whose decision was decisive.
[4 marks — 2 marks for identifying a clear reason interpretations differ, 2 marks for supporting it with evidence from the sources or context.]

lessons.title: Operation Desert Storm and the End of the 1991 War

before.content_html:
17 January 1991 — The War Begins

The 15 January deadline expired with Iraqi forces still in Kuwait. At about 2.30am Baghdad time on 17 January 1991, coalition aircraft began the air phase of Operation Desert Storm. The opening night sent F-117 stealth fighters, Tomahawk cruise missiles and B-52 bombers against Iraqi command bunkers, air defences and the electricity grid. Television viewers around the world watched live as anti-aircraft tracer fire arced over Baghdad — the first war broadcast in real time.

Coalition commander General Norman Schwarzkopf had built his plan around five weeks of air supremacy followed by a short, decisive ground campaign. Air supremacy was achieved within days. Iraq’s Soviet-supplied air defences proved no match for stealth aircraft and electronic warfare; many Iraqi pilots simply flew their aircraft to Iran rather than fight. By the start of the ground war on 24 February, the coalition had flown around 100,000 sorties and the much-vaunted Iraqi army had been bombed for 38 consecutive days.

Key Fact

Operation Desert Storm ran from 17 January to 28 February 1991. The air phase lasted 38 days and roughly 100,000 sorties. The ground phase lasted just 100 hours, ending in a ceasefire on 28 February. Coalition combat deaths totalled around 392; Iraqi military deaths are estimated in the tens of thousands.

Scuds, Patriots and the Israel Question

Saddam knew he could not win an air war, so he tried to fracture the coalition. Iraqi Scud missiles rained on Tel Aviv, Haifa and Riyadh from the second night of the war. Around 42 Scuds hit Israel; another 46 hit Saudi Arabia, including a missile that struck a US barracks at Dhahran on 25 February killing 28 American soldiers.

The Israeli question was the war’s greatest political danger. If Israel retaliated, the Arab partners in the coalition might feel forced to leave. Bush’s administration begged Israel to hold back, sending Patriot anti-missile batteries and crews to Tel Aviv as a gesture. Patriot effectiveness was patchy — many missiles missed, some intercepts caused additional damage as debris fell — but politically the symbolism worked. Israel did not strike back. The coalition held.

Live television coverage from CNN journalists in Baghdad gave the conflict an immediacy no previous war had carried. Pentagon press conferences showed gun-camera footage of laser-guided bombs hitting bunker doorways and ventilation shafts. The reality was that precision-guided munitions made up only around 7–9% of the bombs dropped — the rest were unguided ‘dumb’ bombs — but the imagery shaped the world’s impression that this was a clean, technological war. The Amiriyah shelter strike on 13 February 1991, which killed several hundred Iraqi civilians sheltering from air raids, complicated that image.

100 Hours: The Ground War and the Highway of Death

The ground campaign began at 4am local time on 24 February 1991. Schwarzkopf’s plan, the so-called ‘left hook’, sent VII Corps and XVIII Airborne Corps wide to the west into Iraqi territory while marines pinned Iraqi forces at the Kuwaiti border. Within 36 hours coalition forces had cut the Iraqi army’s line of retreat and were destroying Republican Guard armoured units in southern Iraq.

As the rout developed, Iraqi columns retreating from Kuwait City along the road to Basra were caught by coalition aircraft on the night of 26–27 February. The result, the so-called Highway of Death, was a column of burnt-out vehicles, military and civilian, stretching for kilometres. Photographs of the wreckage, broadcast worldwide, raised concerns even within the Bush administration that the war was tipping from liberation into slaughter. Bush ordered a ceasefire on 28 February at 8am local time, after exactly 100 hours of ground combat.

The Safwan Ceasefire and the Decision Not to March on Baghdad

On 3 March 1991, Schwarzkopf met Iraqi generals at Safwan airfield to set ceasefire terms. Iraq accepted the UN resolutions, agreed to stop firing and pull back. Bush had already taken the larger decision: not to march on Baghdad. The UN mandate covered the liberation of Kuwait, not the overthrow of Saddam. Removing him would have shattered Arab support, risked Iraq fragmenting into civil war, and left coalition troops responsible for an occupation no one had planned. Within days, however, that calculation began to look different.

Encouraged by Bush’s rhetoric inviting the Iraqi people to take matters into their own hands, Shia communities in the south and Kurdish communities in the north rose against the regime in March 1991. Saddam’s Republican Guard had survived the war largely intact and now turned on the rebels. Helicopters that the ceasefire had allowed Iraq to keep flying for ‘internal’ reasons were used to gun down Shia fighters in Basra and Najaf. The uprisings were crushed within weeks, with tens of thousands killed. The coalition had stopped at the border; its absence was the difference between the rebels’ victory and their slaughter.

A common error is to assume that ‘winning the Gulf War’ meant removing Saddam. He stayed in power for another twelve years. The military victory expelled Iraq from Kuwait but left the regime intact, the Republican Guard largely undamaged, and the chemical-weapons stocks unaccounted for. Britain, France and the United States imposed no-fly zones over northern Iraq from April 1991 (Operation Provide Comfort) and southern Iraq from August 1992 (Operation Southern Watch) to protect Kurds and Shia. UN sanctions tightened. Twelve years of containment, weapons inspections and intermittent air strikes followed — until 2003.

Arab Reactions and the Politics of Victory

The Arab world was divided. Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Syria and the smaller Gulf states celebrated the liberation of Kuwait and the discrediting of Saddam. Jordan, Yemen and the Palestine Liberation Organisation had sided with Iraq, partly because of Saddam’s rhetoric linking Kuwait to the Palestinian cause. Their populations, fed by anti-American media coverage, were sympathetic to Saddam even as their states were not. The fault lines exposed in 1990–91 — pro-Western Gulf monarchies versus poorer republics with restive populations — would shape regional politics for decades.

Key Fact

Desert Storm achieved its UN mandate — Kuwait was liberated — but it left enormous problems unresolved: Saddam still in power, Shia and Kurdish uprisings crushed, the Republican Guard intact, chemical weapons unaccounted for and Arab populations split between celebration and resentment. The military victory was complete; the political settlement was thin.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Operation Desert Storm (17 January – 28 February 1991) combined a 38-day air campaign with a 100-hour ground war that liberated Kuwait at a cost of around 392 coalition combat deaths.
  • Bush stopped at the Iraqi border because the UN mandate covered Kuwait, not regime change — a decision reinforced by the political need to keep Arab partners on side.
  • The military victory left major problems unresolved: Saddam survived, the Shia and Kurdish uprisings of spring 1991 were crushed, no-fly zones became a twelve-year holding pattern, and Arab opinion was deeply split.
before.exam_tip_html: For a 16-mark source-based essay, examiners want a substantiated overall judgement, not a balance sheet. On Desert Storm, judgements typically weigh military success (Kuwait liberated, coalition held, 392 coalition dead) against political failure (Saddam survives, Shia and Kurds crushed, regional fault lines exposed). Invent credible source provenance — for example, a 1991 RUSI briefing on coalition airpower for the military side, and a 2016 IISS retrospective on the ceasefire’s long shadow for the political side — and integrate your own knowledge with both. Reach a clear judgement: did the operation achieve its stated aims even if it failed to settle the region?

practice_questions.text: Source A is a January 1991 briefing by a senior officer of the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) on coalition airpower in the opening week of Desert Storm. Source B is a 2016 retrospective from the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) reviewing the 1991 ceasefire's long-term consequences. Study the two sources. 'Operation Desert Storm achieved its aims.' How far do these sources support this view? In your answer use the sources, your own knowledge and contextual judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Support for the statement: Source A documents air supremacy within days, the ineffectiveness of Iraqi defences, and the success of the 38-day air campaign in degrading Iraqi forces.
• Support: Kuwait was liberated within 100 hours of ground combat; coalition combat deaths were limited to around 392; the UN mandate of Resolution 678 was fulfilled.
• Counter: Source B emphasises that Saddam stayed in power for twelve more years, the Republican Guard survived intact, and Shia and Kurdish uprisings were crushed in spring 1991.
• Counter: chemical-weapons stocks were unaccounted for, no-fly zones became a permanent commitment, and the regional fault lines exposed in 1990–91 fed directly into later conflicts.
• Provenance and reliability: a contemporary RUSI briefing reflects optimism of the moment; the 2016 IISS retrospective has hindsight but also reflects post-Iraq-War caution. Both must be weighed.
• Judgement: the operation achieved its stated UN aims (expel Iraq from Kuwait) but failed to deliver a stable political settlement — a partial victory rather than a complete one.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement integrating sources, provenance and own knowledge. Secure: Clear argument with both sides supported by evidence. Developing: Some argument with evidence; provenance treatment limited. Emerging: Description of events with limited engagement with the question.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the air campaign in Operation Desert Storm.

• 38 consecutive days of bombing from 17 January 1991, totalling around 100,000 coalition sorties against Iraqi military and infrastructure targets.
• Use of stealth aircraft (F-117) and cruise missiles (Tomahawk) against high-value targets such as command bunkers and air-defence sites.
• Iraqi Scud missile attacks targeting Israel and Saudi Arabia, met by Patriot anti-missile batteries deployed to keep Israel out of the war.
• Live television coverage including CNN reporting from Baghdad, making this the first war broadcast in real time.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 1 for development with specific detail.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of George H. W. Bush's decision not to advance on Baghdad in 1991.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the decision preserved the UN mandate (limited to liberating Kuwait) and kept Arab partners — particularly Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Syria — inside the coalition.
• It allowed Saddam to crush the Shia and Kurdish uprisings of spring 1991, with helicopter gunships destroying rebel forces while coalition troops watched from the border.
• Significance over time: it locked in twelve years of containment via no-fly zones, sanctions and weapons inspections, with regular flashpoints throughout the 1990s.
• It became a key reference point in 2003 — supporters of the Iraq War argued it had been a mistake to leave Saddam in place; critics argued the 1991 restraint had been correct and 2003 was the error.
[8 marks — Mastering: Significance evaluated at the time and over the period with concrete detail. Secure: Two clear significances with development. Developing: One developed and one undeveloped point. Emerging: Description of the decision with limited reference to significance.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Arab reactions to Saddam's invasion of Kuwait were similar or different across the region.
