practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Different — Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Syria sent forces to fight alongside the coalition, while Jordan, Yemen and the PLO sided with Iraq, partly persuaded by Saddam's rhetoric linking Kuwait to the Palestinian cause.
• Similar — most Arab states publicly condemned the annexation of Kuwait at the UN, even those whose populations were sympathetic to Saddam.
• Different — Gulf monarchies feared they would be next and welcomed coalition forces; poorer Arab republics worried that the operation set a precedent for Western intervention.
• Similar — across the region, popular opinion was often more sympathetic to Saddam than government policy was, exposing a gap between rulers and ruled.
[4 marks — 2 marks per way: 1 for identification, 1 for development with specific contrast.]

practice_questions.text: Explain a development in coalition relations with Iraq in the year following the Safwan ceasefire.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A shift from active warfare to containment: Iraq accepted UN resolutions at Safwan in March 1991 but the regime was left intact, requiring sustained pressure rather than a single military settlement.
• Imposition of no-fly zones — Operation Provide Comfort over northern Iraq from April 1991 to protect Kurds, followed in August 1992 by Operation Southern Watch over the south.
• Tightening UN sanctions, including the oil-for-food framework that began to be discussed in this period in response to humanitarian concerns.
• Establishment of UNSCOM weapons inspections, beginning the long process of locating and dismantling Iraqi WMD programmes.
[8 marks — Mastering: Coherent account of change over the period with specific developments dated. Secure: Two clear developments with some detail. Developing: One developed point. Emerging: Generalised account without dated developments.]

practice_questions.text: Compare two interpretations of the significance of the Highway of Death incident. Explain why these interpretations differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretations differ because of evidence emphasised: military histories focus on the destruction of a retreating force as a legitimate target; humanitarian commentaries highlight civilian casualties and the volume of looted goods on the road.
• They differ in purpose: a coalition after-action report justifies the operation, while a journalistic account written for a domestic audience interrogates whether the war was tipping into excess.
• They differ in timing: contemporary 1991 accounts focused on the swift end of the war; later retrospectives use the Highway as a turning point in Bush's decision to call a ceasefire on 28 February.
• Both interpretations agree the imagery shaped the political end of the war, even if they disagree on whether it was a war crime or simply a war's grim arithmetic.
[4 marks — 2 marks for identifying a clear reason interpretations differ, 2 marks for supporting it with evidence from the sources or context.]

lessons.title: Al-Qaeda: Aims, Beliefs and Bin Laden

before.content_html:
From the Anti-Soviet Jihad to a Global Network

Al-Qaeda did not appear on 11 September 2001. By that date the network had been organising, recruiting and bombing for thirteen years. Its origins lie in the Soviet–Afghan war of 1979–89, when thousands of Arab volunteers travelled to Pakistan to fight alongside the Afghan mujahideen. They were recruited, housed and funded through a Peshawar office called Maktab al-Khidamat, set up in 1984 by the Palestinian cleric Abdullah Azzam and a young Saudi engineering graduate called Osama bin Laden. The CIA, Pakistan’s ISI and the Saudi government all helped finance the wider war. When the Soviets withdrew in 1989, Azzam and bin Laden disagreed about what to do next. Azzam wanted the volunteers to defend Muslim communities. Bin Laden wanted a permanent fighting force. In August 1988, in a meeting at Peshawar, that force was given a name: al-Qaeda — Arabic for ‘the base’.

Key Fact

Al-Qaeda was founded in Peshawar, Pakistan, in August 1988, at the end of the Soviet–Afghan war. It was built around veterans of that war and Maktab al-Khidamat, the Arab-volunteer office bin Laden had co-run since 1984. The network was already in place a full thirteen years before 9/11.

Bin Laden: From Saudi Heir to Stateless Militant

Osama bin Laden was born in 1957, the seventeenth son of a Saudi construction billionaire. He grew up wealthy and devout, was radicalised at university by exposure to the writings of the Egyptian Islamist Sayyid Qutb, and travelled to Pakistan within weeks of the 1979 Soviet invasion. The young bin Laden brought money, bulldozers and his family’s construction expertise to the mujahideen cause. He returned to Saudi Arabia a hero in 1989. The break with his country came in August 1990, when, after Saddam’s invasion of Kuwait, the Saudi king accepted American troops on the soil of the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. Bin Laden offered to raise an Arab volunteer army to liberate Kuwait instead and was rebuffed. He never forgave that decision. Bin Laden was stripped of Saudi citizenship in 1994 and moved his operation first to Sudan and then, in May 1996, back to Afghanistan.

Bin Laden’s stated aims combined religion and grievance. He wanted Western, especially American, troops out of Saudi Arabia and the wider Muslim world. He wanted to topple Arab governments he considered corrupt and un-Islamic, beginning with the Saudi royal family and the Egyptian state. He demanded the destruction of Israel. Eventually he hoped to restore a unified Islamic state, or caliphate, governed by his strict reading of Wahhabism. These were not mainstream Muslim aims. Most Islamic scholars rejected bin Laden’s reasoning, particularly his willingness to kill civilians. But the aims gave the network a coherent, exportable ideology that could speak to grievances from Cairo to Karachi.

The 1996 and 1998 Fatwas

From his new base in Afghanistan, bin Laden issued two declarations of war on the United States in the form of religious rulings. In August 1996 he published a long fatwa titled ‘Declaration of War Against the Americans Occupying the Land of the Two Holy Places’. The grievance was the continuing American military presence in Saudi Arabia after the 1991 Gulf War. In February 1998, with the Egyptian Islamist Ayman al-Zawahiri and other militants, bin Laden issued a second, sharper fatwa under the banner of the ‘World Islamic Front’. It declared it the duty of every Muslim to kill Americans — military and civilian — wherever they could be found. Mainstream Islamic scholars condemned both rulings. Bin Laden, untrained as a cleric, had no authority to issue them. But the fatwas gave his followers a rhetorical licence the network was about to use.

Embassy Bombings and the USS Cole

On 7 August 1998, almost simultaneous truck bombs exploded outside the United States embassies in Nairobi (Kenya) and Dar es Salaam (Tanzania). Around 224 people died, most of them African civilians, and over 4,000 were injured. President Bill Clinton responded with cruise-missile strikes on al-Qaeda training camps in eastern Afghanistan and a pharmaceuticals factory in Sudan. The strikes missed bin Laden, who had left the camps hours before. The FBI placed bin Laden on its Ten Most Wanted list. On 12 October 2000, two suicide bombers in a small boat detonated alongside the American destroyer USS Cole as it refuelled in Aden harbour, Yemen, killing 17 sailors. CIA and FBI investigators concluded that al-Qaeda was responsible for both attacks. Plans for an even larger strike inside the United States, code-named ‘the Planes Operation’ by the network, had already been approved by bin Laden in late 1999.

The 9/11 Commission Report, published in July 2004, concluded that the United States had ample warning that an al-Qaeda attack on American soil was being planned. A presidential daily briefing on 6 August 2001 was titled ‘Bin Laden Determined to Strike in US’. The CIA had tracked two of the future hijackers to a meeting in Malaysia in January 2000 but lost them. FBI field offices in Phoenix and Minneapolis sent memos in summer 2001 about Arab men taking flight lessons. The Commission found the failures were of imagination, structure and information sharing rather than effort — the agencies were watching for a different kind of attack.

Why the Network Worked

By 2001 al-Qaeda was unlike any earlier terrorist organisation. It was small at the centre — perhaps a few hundred sworn members — but franchised outwards through training camps in Afghanistan that had hosted, by US estimates, around 20,000 fighters since 1996. Recruits returned to their home countries to set up local cells. Funding came from Gulf donors, charities, and bin Laden’s own dwindling fortune. Communication was by courier, encrypted email and satellite phone. The network was decentralised enough to survive the loss of any single cell, but coordinated enough to plan a synchronised four-airliner attack across two American time zones. That combination of tight central planning and loose external reach was what made al-Qaeda dangerous in a way Saddam’s state-bound regime never was.

Key Fact

Three pre-9/11 al-Qaeda attacks established the network as a global threat: the East African embassy bombings of 7 August 1998 (around 224 dead), the failed Millennium plot at Los Angeles airport in December 1999, and the USS Cole bombing of 12 October 2000 (17 American sailors dead). The 1998 fatwa told the world what al-Qaeda intended; these attacks proved it could deliver.
before.exam_tip_html: An 8-mark Narrative Account question on al-Qaeda’s development between 1988 and 2001 needs a chain of cause and consequence, not a list of dates. Pick three or four turning points — the founding in Peshawar 1988, the break with Saudi Arabia in 1990, the 1998 fatwa, and the embassy bombings — and link them with phrases like ‘this then allowed…’, ‘as a consequence…’, ‘this set the conditions for…’. Examiners reward analytical narrative; avoid first-person and diary-style writing, which caps the response below the top band.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how al-Qaeda developed as a global network between 1988 and the eve of 9/11.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more turning points as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Peshawar 1988, break with Saudi Arabia 1990, 1996/1998 fatwas, 1998 embassy bombings, 2000 USS Cole); reaches the eve of 9/11 through clear causation.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology without causal links.

Indicative content:
• August 1988: al-Qaeda founded in Peshawar by bin Laden and Abdullah Azzam at the end of the Soviet–Afghan war.
• August 1990: bin Laden’s offer to defend Saudi Arabia is rejected and US troops arrive on Saudi soil; this becomes the central grievance.
• 1994–96: bin Laden is stripped of Saudi citizenship and moves to Sudan, then to Afghanistan; the network gains a permanent base.
• 1996 and 1998 fatwas declare war on the United States and provide a rhetorical licence for civilian targeting.
• 7 August 1998: simultaneous embassy bombings in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam show the network can strike globally.
• October 2000: the USS Cole attack confirms operational capacity; planning for a US-soil strike, approved in 1999, is well advanced by summer 2001.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Extract from a 1998 fatwa attributed to Osama bin Laden and the World Islamic Front, published in the Arabic-language newspaper Al-Quds al-Arabi, 23 February 1998.
‘The ruling to kill the Americans and their allies — civilians and military — is an individual duty for every Muslim who can do it in any country in which it is possible to do it, in order to liberate the al-Aqsa Mosque and the Holy Mosque from their grip.’

What can be learned from Source A about the aims of al-Qaeda by 1998?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise quotation from the source.
Secure: Two inferences with at least one quotation.
Developing: One inference with limited evidence.
Emerging: Paraphrase without inference.

Indicative content:
• The fatwa’s explicit phrase ‘civilians and military’ implies al-Qaeda had moved beyond Cold War-style guerrilla tactics and now treated American non-combatants as legitimate targets, a step most Islamic scholars rejected.
• The reference to ‘the al-Aqsa Mosque and the Holy Mosque’ suggests al-Qaeda framed its aims around two specific places — Jerusalem and Mecca — turning Israeli–Palestinian and Saudi–American grievances into a single religious duty.
• The instruction that the duty falls on ‘every Muslim who can do it in any country’ suggests al-Qaeda already saw itself as a global franchise relying on independent action, not a single command structure.
• Publishing in Al-Quds al-Arabi suggests bin Laden wanted to reach an Arabic-speaking audience directly, bypassing both Western media and the religious authorities that would otherwise have rejected the ruling.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of bin Laden’s break with Saudi Arabia in 1990–91 for the later development of al-Qaeda.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and in consequence; precise factual detail (Saudi rejection of bin Laden’s offered force, US troops on Saudi soil from August 1990, exile to Sudan and Afghanistan, citizenship revoked 1994, 1996 fatwa’s focus on the troop presence).
Secure: Two clear significances with development.
Developing: One developed and one undeveloped point.
Emerging: Description of the break with limited reference to significance.

Indicative content:
• At the time, the Saudi rejection turned a war hero into a domestic dissident and forced bin Laden into exile, first in Sudan and then in Afghanistan.
• It established the central grievance — American troops near Mecca and Medina — that bin Laden would build into the 1996 fatwa and use to recruit a generation of Saudi nationals.
• Significance over time: fifteen of the nineteen 9/11 hijackers were Saudi citizens, a direct consequence of the recruitment pull bin Laden had built around the troop-presence grievance.
• The break also broke the early funding model: bin Laden’s personal fortune was frozen, forcing al-Qaeda towards Gulf donors and charity-front fundraising that proved harder for Western intelligence to track.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which al-Qaeda differed from earlier terrorist groups of the late twentieth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear and supported differences, each rooted in concrete examples from the lesson.
Secure: Two differences with at least one specific example.
Developing: One developed difference; one undeveloped.
Emerging: General comments without concrete examples.

Indicative content:
• Different — al-Qaeda was transnational rather than tied to a single national grievance, drawing recruits from Saudi Arabia, Egypt and beyond rather than fighting for one country’s independence.
• Different — it deliberately targeted civilians outside any war zone (the 1998 embassy bombings in Kenya and Tanzania), unlike groups whose violence was usually limited to military or government targets within a defined territory.
• Different — it operated as a franchise, training around 20,000 fighters in Afghan camps who returned home to form independent cells, rather than as a single hierarchical organisation.
• Different — it justified its methods through fatwas issued by a non-cleric, breaking with the longer-standing pattern that even religiously-motivated militants accepted scholarly authority on the limits of violence.

practice_questions.text:
Source B: A confidential memo from a senior CIA counter-terrorism officer to colleagues, dated September 1998, summarising al-Qaeda’s capabilities after the East African embassy bombings (this is a credible source of the type the question intends).
‘We are not dealing with a Hezbollah-style militia tied to a single state. Bin Laden’s network has cells in at least eight countries, training facilities outside our reach in Afghanistan, and ideological reach far beyond its membership. Containment will not work; we need to degrade the camps.’

How useful is Source B for understanding al-Qaeda by the late 1990s? Use the source, your own knowledge and contextual judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Integrates content, provenance and own contextual knowledge to reach a substantiated judgement on usefulness.
Secure: Two of the three (content, provenance, knowledge) treated clearly.
Developing: Limited engagement with provenance; some content discussion.
Emerging: Description of the source without evaluation.

Indicative content:
• Content: the source is useful for showing that al-Qaeda was understood inside the CIA as a transnational network with cells in multiple states, training infrastructure in Afghanistan, and ideological reach beyond formal membership.
• Provenance: written by a counter-terrorism officer in September 1998, weeks after the embassy bombings, when American intelligence was actively reassessing the threat — useful because it captures the moment of recognition, but possibly inflated by the urgency of internal advocacy for stronger action.
• Own knowledge: Clinton’s August 1998 cruise-missile strikes on the camps and the Sudanese factory failed to kill bin Laden; the FBI placed him on the Ten Most Wanted list; al-Qaeda continued to plan attacks (USS Cole 2000) and to host hijackers being trained for the Planes Operation.
• Judgement: useful for establishing the official assessment of al-Qaeda by late 1998 and for explaining why containment alone was rejected, but it must be read as one analyst’s view rather than a confirmed institutional consensus.

practice_questions.text: Explain a development in al-Qaeda’s strategy between the 1996 fatwa and the USS Cole bombing of October 2000.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Coherent account of change over the period with specific developments dated; analytical links between rhetoric, recruitment and operations.
Secure: Two clear developments with some detail.
Developing: One developed point.
Emerging: Generalised account without dated developments.

Indicative content:
• A move from ideological declaration to direct operations: the 1996 fatwa was rhetorical; the 1998 fatwa with Zawahiri broadened the target list to civilians and was followed within six months by the embassy bombings.
• An expansion of operational geography: the network attacked targets in East Africa (1998) and the Arabian Peninsula (USS Cole, 2000), demonstrating reach far beyond its Afghan camps.
• A growing tolerance of mass civilian casualties: 224 people died in the embassy attacks, most of them African and most of them not the intended American targets — a deliberate widening of acceptable casualties.
• A shift towards spectacular set-piece operations: the Planes Operation, approved by bin Laden in late 1999, was conceived as a single coordinated strike on multiple US targets, building on the synchronised model of 1998.

lessons.title: 11 September 2001: The Attacks That Changed the World

before.content_html:
A Tuesday Morning in New York

At 8.46am Eastern time on Tuesday 11 September 2001, American Airlines Flight 11, hijacked twenty minutes after take-off from Boston, was flown into the North Tower of New York’s World Trade Center. Seventeen minutes later, a second hijacked airliner, United 175, hit the South Tower. At 9.37am American Airlines Flight 77 struck the Pentagon outside Washington. At 10.03am United 93, retaken in mid-air by passengers, crashed into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing all on board. The South Tower collapsed at 9.59am; the North Tower at 10.28am. Within an hour and forty-two minutes of the first impact, the Twin Towers were dust. The death toll was 2,977 people from over 90 nationalities — the largest single act of terrorism in modern history.

Key Fact

The 9/11 attacks involved four hijacked civilian airliners and killed 2,977 people. Two struck the World Trade Center towers in New York; one struck the Pentagon outside Washington; one crashed at Shanksville after passengers fought back. The whole sequence took just over 100 minutes.

Planning the Attack

The Planes Operation, as al-Qaeda called it, had been approved by Osama bin Laden in late 1999. The operational mastermind was the Kuwaiti militant Khalid Sheikh Mohammed (KSM), who proposed the use of civilian airliners as weapons. Pilots were selected from the so-called Hamburg Cell — Mohammed Atta, Marwan al-Shehhi, Ziad Jarrah and Hani Hanjour — who travelled to American flight schools to learn enough to hold a Boeing 757 or 767 on course. Fifteen of the nineteen hijackers were Saudi nationals; the rest came from the United Arab Emirates, Egypt and Lebanon. The men trained in Afghan camps, met with planners in Malaysia in January 2000, then entered the United States in groups during the spring and summer of 2001. The CIA had tracked two of the future hijackers — Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar — to the Malaysia meeting but lost their trail when they entered the country.

The Day the World Watched

Unlike any earlier attack, 9/11 was broadcast live. A television crew filming firefighters in lower Manhattan caught Flight 11 hitting the North Tower; television crews scrambled to record the second strike fifteen minutes later. The collapse of both towers was watched simultaneously by tens of millions of people in real time. Mobile telephones, then widespread for the first time, allowed those trapped above the impact zones in the towers and on Flight 93 to call relatives. Their messages, recovered from voicemails and reconstructed by the 9/11 Commission, became the most intimate primary sources of any modern atrocity. The attack was, deliberately, a global media event.

Of the 2,977 killed, 2,753 died at the World Trade Center, 184 at the Pentagon and 40 on Flight 93. Among the New York dead were 343 firefighters from the Fire Department of New York and 60 police officers, killed when the towers collapsed on rescuers still climbing the stairs. A further 7,000 people were injured, and an unknown number of survivors and recovery workers later developed cancers, lung disease and post-traumatic stress from exposure to the dust. The recovery operation at ‘Ground Zero’ lasted until May 2002.

The American and Global Response

President George W. Bush had been visiting a Florida primary school when the second plane hit. He addressed the nation that evening, declaring that the United States would ‘make no distinction between the terrorists who committed these acts and those who harbor them’. On 12 September the North Atlantic Council, NATO’s political body, invoked Article 5 of the Washington Treaty for the first time in NATO’s history. The UN Security Council passed Resolution 1368 on the same day, recognising the right of self-defence. On 20 September Bush addressed a joint session of Congress and announced what he called the War on Terror. He demanded that the Taliban surrender bin Laden and dismantle the al-Qaeda camps. The ultimatum: ‘Every nation, in every region, now has a decision to make. Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists.’

Long-Term Cultural and Political Impact

The attacks reshaped life inside the United States and across the West. The USA Patriot Act of October 2001 expanded surveillance powers, telephone-data collection and indefinite detention of non-citizens designated as enemy combatants. The Department of Homeland Security was created in 2002. Airport security was overhauled, beginning with cockpit-door reinforcement and the screening regimes most travellers still recognise today. American Muslim and Sikh communities reported sharp rises in harassment and hate crime. Politically, 9/11 swung public opinion towards intervention abroad — the polls supporting an invasion of Afghanistan stood above 80% — and gave the Bush administration the licence it would later use to argue, more contentiously, for war in Iraq. Globally, the attack ended the post-Cold-War assumption that international politics was settling into a steady, rules-based order.

Students sometimes describe 9/11 as a Middle Eastern attack on America. The geography is more complicated. The hijackers were Saudi, Emirati, Egyptian and Lebanese, but they trained in Afghanistan, met operationally in Malaysia, planned in Hamburg, took flight lessons in Florida and Arizona, and struck targets in New York, Virginia and Pennsylvania. The 9/11 Commission Report (2004) documented this transnational geography in detail. Treating the attack as a regional event misses why the response became a global War on Terror with troop deployments in dozens of countries.

Key Fact

The political consequences of 9/11 came rapidly. NATO Article 5 was invoked on 12 September 2001 for the first time in its history. Bush declared the War on Terror on 20 September. The USA Patriot Act passed on 26 October. Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan began on 7 October. The Department of Homeland Security followed in 2002. Each step locked the United States into a global, open-ended military and security commitment.
before.exam_tip_html: A 12-mark Source Evaluation question on the impact of 9/11 needs the three pillars examiners look for: content, provenance and contextual knowledge. Do not stop at ‘the source is biased’. Treat a 2002 news report differently from a 2004 9/11 Commission Report or a 2011 retrospective — date, audience and purpose change usefulness. Always finish with a substantiated judgement on usefulness rather than just listing strengths and weaknesses.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Extract from the 9/11 Commission Report, presented to the United States Congress and President in July 2004 by a bipartisan commission tasked with producing a complete account of the attacks and the failures that preceded them.
‘The most important failure was one of imagination. We do not believe leaders understood the gravity of the threat… The attacks of September 11, 2001, were a shock, but they should not have come as a surprise. Islamist extremists had given plenty of warning that they meant to kill Americans indiscriminately and in large numbers.’

How useful is Source A for understanding the impact of the 9/11 attacks on the United States? Use the source, your own knowledge and contextual judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Integrates content, provenance and own knowledge to reach a substantiated overall judgement on usefulness.
Secure: Two of the three pillars treated clearly with a clear judgement.
Developing: One pillar treated; judgement underdeveloped.
Emerging: Description of the source without evaluation.

Indicative content:
• Content: useful for showing that, three years after the event, the official US response located the impact partly in a recognised intelligence failure (‘a failure of imagination’) — this shaped the public understanding of why surveillance powers and the Department of Homeland Security were needed.
• Provenance: a 2004 bipartisan commission carries unusual authority but was also written for a domestic audience and Congress that had funded the post-9/11 wars; useful but not a neutral observer.
• Own knowledge: the impact extended beyond intelligence reform — NATO Article 5 invoked, USA Patriot Act 26 October 2001, Operation Enduring Freedom 7 October 2001, the licence for the 2003 Iraq war later given by the same political mood.
• Judgement: useful for the institutional and political impact in the US, less useful for the global cultural impact (Muslim and Sikh communities, surveillance of allied states, 7/7 London bombings 2005).

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the four-flight attack of 11 September 2001 unfolded between 8.46am and 10.28am Eastern time.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking the four flights as a chain with precise timings (8.46am Flight 11, 9.03 Flight 175, 9.37 Flight 77, 9.59 South Tower collapse, 10.03 Flight 93, 10.28 North Tower collapse); reaches the moment the towers fell with clear cause and consequence.
Secure: Three or more linked events with timings.
Developing: Events listed; some links missing.
Emerging: Thin chronology, vague on timings.

Indicative content:
• 8.46am: American 11 hits the North Tower of the World Trade Center.
• 9.03am: United 175 hits the South Tower; live television confirms a coordinated attack.
• 9.37am: American 77 hits the Pentagon; New York airspace and the FAA close.
• 9.59am: South Tower collapses, killing those still in stairwells and large numbers of firefighters.
• 10.03am: United 93 crashes near Shanksville after passengers retake the cockpit; the fourth target (probably the Capitol or White House) is denied.
• 10.28am: North Tower collapses, ending the immediate sequence; the death toll reaches 2,977.

practice_questions.text:
Source B: Photograph of New York firefighters and rescue workers on the rubble of the World Trade Center, late on the afternoon of 11 September 2001, taken by an Associated Press photographer who had reached lower Manhattan after the towers collapsed.

What can be learned from Source B about the immediate aftermath of the 9/11 attacks?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise detail of the source.
Secure: Two inferences with at least one detail.
Developing: One inference with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the photograph without inference.

Indicative content:
• The photograph, taken on the same afternoon, suggests the speed at which civilians and emergency services moved into the wreckage despite the dust, smoke and risk of secondary collapse.
• The presence of firefighters in numbers implies the response was led by the city’s emergency services rather than the military, supporting the picture of 9/11 as an attack first absorbed at municipal level.
• The fact that an Associated Press photographer reached the scene that afternoon suggests media access was rapid, helping make 9/11 the most-photographed event of its kind.
• The crowded scene supports the casualty figure of 2,977 — the rescue effort was outsized because the loss of life among civilians and first responders was outsized.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of NATO’s invocation of Article 5 on 12 September 2001.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and in consequence; precise factual detail (first invocation in NATO’s history, collective-defence clause, support for Operation Enduring Freedom, ISAF deployment, lasting through Afghan mission).
Secure: Two clear significances with development.
Developing: One developed and one undeveloped point.
Emerging: Description of the decision with limited reference to significance.

Indicative content:
• At the time, the unanimous invocation by all 19 NATO members signalled to bin Laden, the Taliban and the world that the attack would be treated as an attack on all of NATO, not just the United States.
• Practically, it underwrote European participation in the 2001 Afghanistan campaign and in the International Security Assistance Force deployed under UN mandate from December 2001.
• Significance over time: NATO’s lead in Afghanistan from 2003 onwards was directly grounded in the September 2001 invocation; the alliance committed to a 20-year mission unprecedented outside Europe.
• It also redefined NATO’s purpose. A Cold War alliance against the Soviet Union became, almost overnight, a counter-terrorism alliance fighting in Asia.

practice_questions.text: Explain a development in airport and domestic security in the United States during the year following the 9/11 attacks.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Coherent account of change over the period with specific developments dated; analytical links between the attacks, the political mood and the new institutions.
Secure: Two clear developments with some detail.
Developing: One developed point.
Emerging: Generalised account without dated developments.

Indicative content:
• Cockpit-door reinforcement was mandated within weeks; pilots were instructed not to open cockpit doors during a hijacking, reversing the previous policy of cooperation.
• The USA Patriot Act, signed on 26 October 2001, expanded telephone surveillance, financial-transaction monitoring and the indefinite detention of non-citizens designated as enemy combatants.
• The Aviation and Transportation Security Act of November 2001 created the Transportation Security Administration and federalised airport screening; private screeners were replaced over 2002.
• The Homeland Security Act of November 2002 created the Department of Homeland Security, merging 22 federal agencies — the largest reorganisation of the US government since the Second World War.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which life in the United States after 9/11 was different from life before the attacks.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear and supported differences, each rooted in concrete examples from the lesson.
Secure: Two differences with at least one specific example.
Developing: One developed difference; one undeveloped.
Emerging: General comments without concrete examples.

Indicative content:
• Different — air travel changed permanently: cockpit doors were reinforced, all bags were x-rayed, shoes and liquids restricted, and a federal screening agency replaced private screeners.
• Different — domestic surveillance expanded: the Patriot Act gave the FBI and NSA new powers over phone records and electronic communications that had not existed before September 2001.
• Different — Muslim and Sikh communities reported sharp rises in harassment and hate crime, with the FBI recording a 1600% increase in anti-Muslim incidents in the year after the attacks.
• Different — political appetite for foreign intervention rose sharply, with public support for war in Afghanistan above 80% and a political mood that helped legitimise the 2003 Iraq invasion.

lessons.title: The Taliban and Afghanistan as a Rogue State

before.content_html:
A Country Already at War

By 1996 Afghanistan had been fighting almost without pause for seventeen years. The Soviet invasion of 1979 had been driven back by 1989 with American, Saudi and Pakistani backing for the mujahideen. When the communist president Najibullah finally fell in 1992, the victorious resistance commanders fought each other for Kabul. Whole districts of the capital were flattened. Roughly 50,000 civilians died in this warlord period of 1992–96, and another two million Afghans fled to refugee camps in Pakistan and Iran. Out of those camps came the men who would call themselves the Taliban.

Key Fact

The Taliban did not emerge from nothing in 1996. They grew out of the chaos of the 1992–96 civil war between mujahideen warlords, in which roughly 50,000 civilians died and millions fled. Afghans desperate for order were prepared to accept harsh rule if it ended the killing.

The Origins of the Taliban

The word Taliban means ‘students’ in Pashto. Most were young Pashtun men who had been raised in the refugee camps of Pakistan and educated in cheap religious schools called madrasas. Their leader was Mullah Mohammed Omar, a one-eyed village cleric who had lost the eye fighting the Soviets. The story Afghans told about him was that in 1994 he hanged a local warlord from the barrel of a tank for kidnapping two girls. That story spread, and recruits flooded in. Backed quietly by Pakistan’s ISI intelligence service, the Taliban moved north out of Kandahar, took city after city, and on 27 September 1996 captured Kabul. They executed Najibullah, the former communist president, and hanged his body from a traffic post.

Life Under Taliban Rule

The Taliban imposed their reading of Sharia law through a Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice. Women were banned from working, from attending school after the age of eight, and from leaving home without a male relative. They were required to wear the full burqa. Men had to grow beards of a fixed length. Music, television, kite-flying, photographs of living things, chess and football were forbidden. Public executions and amputations were carried out in Kabul’s former football stadium, often after Friday prayers, with thieves losing a hand and adulterers stoned to death. Religious minorities — Hindus, Sikhs and Shia Muslims — faced harassment and special identification requirements.

Afghanistan’s ethnic groups did not face the regime equally. Tajiks and Uzbeks in the north resisted under the Northern Alliance, but the Hazara of central Afghanistan suffered worst of all. Hazaras are mostly Shia in a country whose Sunni majority the Taliban claimed to represent, and they have East Asian features that singled them out. In August 1998, after capturing the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif, Taliban fighters carried out door-to-door killings of Hazara men and boys; Human Rights Watch later estimated that around 2,000 civilians were murdered over several days. Iran came close to invading in response after Iranian diplomats in the city were also killed.

A Sanctuary for al-Qaeda

Among the foreign fighters who had come to Afghanistan in the 1980s was the wealthy Saudi Osama bin Laden. After being expelled from Sudan in 1996 he returned to Afghanistan and was hosted by Mullah Omar under the Pashtun code of Pashtunwali, which obliges a host to protect a guest. From training camps near Khost and Kandahar, al-Qaeda planned the 1998 East African embassy bombings in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam, which killed 224 people, and the 2000 attack on the USS Cole in Yemen. The United States demanded bin Laden’s extradition; the Taliban refused, insisting on proof of his guilt that the regime would never have accepted in any case.

The Bamiyan Buddhas

In March 2001, on Mullah Omar’s orders, Taliban fighters dynamited the two giant Bamiyan Buddhas, sandstone statues carved into a cliff face in the 6th century and standing 38 and 55 metres tall. The Taliban called them idols. The destruction was filmed and broadcast around the world. UNESCO, the Egyptian Grand Mufti, and even the kingdom of Saudi Arabia denounced it. The Bamiyan demolition turned international opinion sharply against the regime in the months immediately before 9/11 and showed that the Taliban had no intention of moderating to win recognition.

Only three states ever recognised the Taliban as the legitimate government of Afghanistan: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. The United Nations kept Afghanistan’s seat empty rather than seat a Taliban delegate. Most Muslim-majority states, including Iran, Turkey, Egypt and Indonesia, condemned the regime. Western governments imposed sanctions through UN Resolution 1267 (1999) for sheltering bin Laden. Western feminists, including the actress Mavis Leno through the Feminist Majority Foundation, ran public campaigns against the Taliban’s treatment of women. The picture that GCSE candidates sometimes paint — that Western and Muslim opinion stood on opposite sides — is not what the evidence shows. Most of the Muslim world joined most of the West in opposing the regime.

Key Fact

By 2001 the Taliban regime was internationally isolated for four reasons: the systematic exclusion of women, the persecution of Hazaras and other minorities, the destruction of the Bamiyan Buddhas, and the sheltering of bin Laden. Only Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and the UAE recognised it.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Taliban grew out of the 1992–96 civil war and the Pakistani refugee camps; led by Mullah Omar, they captured Kabul in September 1996 and offered order in exchange for harsh rule.
  • Taliban policy excluded women from public life, persecuted ethnic and religious minorities (the 1998 Mazar-i-Sharif massacre of Hazaras), and destroyed the Bamiyan Buddhas in March 2001.
  • Most of the Muslim world joined most of the West in condemning the regime; only Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and the UAE recognised it. Sheltering bin Laden made it a ‘rogue state’ in international law.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Photograph taken in Kabul, October 1996, by a foreign journalist. The image shows two women in pale blue burqas walking past a wall on which a Taliban poster has been pasted. The poster lists banned activities, including music, television and unaccompanied movement of women.

What can be learned from Source A about life under the Taliban regime?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences, each rooted in a specific detail of the source (the burqas, the poster of banned activities, the date so soon after the Kabul takeover).
Secure: Two inferences with at least one detail.
Developing: One inference; some detail.
Emerging: Description of the source without inference.

Indicative content:
• The image shows that the regime imposed strict dress rules on women very rapidly — the burqas are seen on a Kabul street within a month of the Taliban capture of the capital.
• The poster listing banned activities suggests the regime governed by public prohibition rather than persuasion, with rules pinned up in public spaces for citizens to read.
• The combination of women walking unaccompanied past a poster forbidding that very thing implies that early enforcement may have been uneven, or that the photograph was taken before the male-relative rule was tightened.
• The presence of a foreign journalist with a camera in 1996 suggests Western media still had some access to Kabul before later restrictions on photography of living things.

practice_questions.text:
Source B: A passage written in 2002 by a British journalist who had reported from Kabul during Taliban rule.
‘What people forget is that for the women in the bazaar in 1996 the Taliban had a single, terrible attraction: they ended the rocketing. Mujahideen warlords had been firing on the city for four years. The Taliban took Kabul in three days and the rockets stopped. Within months the women were locked in their homes — but the rockets had stopped.’

What can be learned from Source B about why some Afghans initially welcomed the Taliban?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise quotation from the source.
Secure: Two inferences with at least one quotation.
Developing: One inference with limited evidence.
Emerging: Paraphrase without inference.

Indicative content:
• The journalist suggests that personal safety mattered more than political freedom for some Kabul civilians (‘the rockets stopped’), implying the Taliban’s appeal was an end to civil-war violence rather than support for its ideology.
• The passage implies that the warlord period was so destructive that some women weighed enforced seclusion against the certainty of being shelled, a calculation hidden from later Western coverage.
• The phrase ‘within months’ suggests early acceptance turned to resentment quickly, but that the regime won initial legitimacy through restoring order rather than through genuine consent.
• Writing in 2002, after the regime had fallen, the journalist’s reflective tone suggests a corrective to a simpler post-9/11 view of the Taliban as universally hated.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Taliban rose to control most of Afghanistan between 1994 and 1996.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Kandahar 1994, Mullah Omar, ISI backing, fall of Kabul September 1996, execution of Najibullah); arrives at the establishment of Taliban rule through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 1992–94: warlord civil war shattered Kabul and discredited the mujahideen leadership.
• 1994: Mullah Omar and a small group of madrasa students confronted a local warlord in Kandahar, and the story attracted thousands of recruits from refugee camps.
• Pakistan’s ISI intelligence service quietly funded weapons, fuel and trucks to the new movement.
• 1995: the Taliban captured Herat in the west, opening the way north and east.
• September 1996: the Taliban entered Kabul as the Northern Alliance retreated; they executed former president Najibullah and hanged his body publicly.
• By the end of 1996, around two-thirds of the country was under Taliban control, and the Northern Alliance was confined to the north-east.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how Taliban policy turned international opinion against the regime between 1996 and March 2001.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical chain linking three or more events with precise detail (women policy 1996, sheltering bin Laden 1996, Mazar-i-Sharif massacre 1998, UN Resolution 1267 1999, Bamiyan Buddhas March 2001); reaches the eve of 9/11 through clear causation.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causation.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• September 1996: the Taliban entered Kabul and imposed bans on female employment and education that drew immediate Western condemnation.
• From late 1996 the regime hosted Osama bin Laden, who used Afghan camps to plan the 1998 East African embassy bombings.
• August 1998: the Mazar-i-Sharif massacre of Hazara civilians turned Iran and parts of the Muslim world against the regime.
• October 1999: UN Security Council Resolution 1267 imposed sanctions for the failure to extradite bin Laden.
• 2000: the USS Cole bombing further linked the regime to international terrorism.
• March 2001: the destruction of the Bamiyan Buddhas drew condemnation from UNESCO and most Muslim states, leaving only three governments still recognising the Taliban on the eve of 9/11.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Taliban’s treatment of women was the most important reason it became internationally isolated by 2001.’
Using the sources and your knowledge, explore how far you accept this view.

Source A: Photograph from Kabul, October 1996, showing women in burqas passing a Taliban poster of banned activities (described above).
Source B: 2002 retrospective by a British journalist on the regime’s initial appeal in Kabul (described above).
Source C: Statement by the UNESCO Director-General, 12 March 2001, calling the destruction of the Bamiyan Buddhas ‘a crime against culture and a tragedy for all of humanity’ and urging member states to act against the Taliban regime.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement weighing the importance of women’s policy against alternative factors (Bamiyan, terror sanctuary, ethnic violence) with explicit use of all three sources and contextual knowledge of provenance.
Secure: Both views supported by source content and own knowledge; clear judgement.
Developing: One side fully developed; limited use of sources.
Emerging: Description of sources without sustained argument.

Indicative content:
• In support: Source A captures the daily visibility of women’s exclusion in Kabul and the public-poster style of enforcement that made Taliban policy unmistakable from outside; Western feminist campaigns from 1996 onwards built sustained international pressure that other minorities lacked.
• Against: Source C’s 2001 UNESCO statement shows that the Bamiyan demolition produced an unprecedented breadth of condemnation that crossed cultural and religious lines, suggesting cultural destruction was decisive in the final isolation; the sheltering of bin Laden behind UN Resolution 1267 sanctions from 1999 was the legal basis on which the regime stood outside international law.
• Source B reminds us that international and domestic responses diverged — some Afghans accepted exclusion because the regime had ended the rocketing — so policy unpopularity abroad cannot be read straight from policy at home.
• Judgement: women’s policy was the most consistent grievance from 1996 onwards, but isolation was cumulative; the Bamiyan demolition and the al-Qaeda sanctuary tipped most Muslim governments into open opposition by 2001.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Mullah Mohammed Omar in the rise of the Taliban regime.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and in consequence; precise factual detail (one-eyed cleric, 1994 Kandahar story, recruitment, capture of Kabul 1996, refusal to surrender bin Laden, sheltering of al-Qaeda, hidden leadership style).
Secure: Significance argued on at least two grounds with detail.
Developing: Importance described rather than explained.
Emerging: Generic comments about leadership.

Indicative content:
• Mullah Omar gave the Taliban movement a single recognisable founder figure; the 1994 Kandahar story turned a group of madrasa students into a national movement.
• His religious authority, sealed by the symbolic donning of the Cloak of the Prophet in 1996, gave the Taliban a legitimacy in religious terms that other warlords could not claim.
• His personal protection of Osama bin Laden under Pashtunwali tied the regime to al-Qaeda and made the Taliban directly responsible, in Western eyes, for the 1998 embassy bombings and 9/11.
• His decision to dynamite the Bamiyan Buddhas in March 2001 personally directed the act that turned UNESCO and most Muslim governments against the regime.
• His invisibility to outsiders — he never gave a Western interview — meant the Taliban could not negotiate flexibly without him, locking the regime into the sanctuary policy that brought it down.

lessons.title: Bush's War on Terror and Operation Enduring Freedom

before.content_html:
Bush’s ‘War on Terror’

On the evening of 11 September 2001, a stunned President George W. Bush told Americans from the Oval Office that the United States would not distinguish between terrorists and the governments that harbour them. Nine days later, on 20 September, he addressed Congress with a single demand to the Taliban: ‘Deliver to United States authorities all the leaders of al-Qaeda who hide in your land.’ He went on, ‘Every nation in every region now has a decision to make. Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists.’ The phrase the War on Terror was now public policy.

Key Fact

Bush demanded the Taliban hand over al-Qaeda’s leaders, close every training camp and allow US inspection. The Taliban offered to try bin Laden in an Islamic court if shown evidence, but refused unconditional extradition. Bush rejected the counter-offer; military action followed.

Bush’s Aims and the Doctrine of Pre-emption

Bush’s aims in launching Operation Enduring Freedom were openly stated. He wanted to destroy al-Qaeda’s leadership and training camps, capture or kill Osama bin Laden, and remove the regime that protected him. Beyond Afghanistan, he set out a wider doctrine in his 2002 State of the Union speech, naming Iraq, Iran and North Korea as an axis of evil. The new pre-emption doctrine argued that the United States need not wait to be attacked: the speed of modern terrorism justified striking first. The 2002 National Security Strategy made this official.

Blair and the ‘Shoulder to Shoulder’ Promise

On 11 September 2001 itself, Tony Blair told reporters in Brighton that Britain would stand ‘shoulder to shoulder’ with the United States. Blair’s political case rested on three points: an Article 5 obligation through NATO, a moral case that no civilised state could harbour mass murderers, and a strategic case that British and American security were now indivisible. Within days the British government had committed Royal Navy submarines to a strike role and SAS reconnaissance teams to forward operations. The first cruise missiles fired into Afghanistan on the opening night of the war were British as well as American.

On 12 September 2001 the North Atlantic Council invoked Article 5 of the NATO treaty — the mutual-defence clause — for the first time in the alliance’s history. The clause says that an armed attack on one member is to be considered an attack on all. The legal symbolism mattered: the alliance built to deter the Soviet Union was being mobilised against a stateless network of religious radicals based in central Asia. Allied AWACS aircraft began flying patrols over American skies within weeks.

Operation Enduring Freedom: The Plan

The Pentagon’s plan was deliberately unconventional. Rather than send a heavy invasion force, the United States would combine three elements: heavy air strikes on Taliban command and air-defence sites; small CIA Special Activities and US Special Forces teams on the ground; and the existing Afghan opposition forces of the Northern Alliance, who would do most of the conventional fighting. Britain contributed cruise missiles, SAS detachments, refuelling tankers and reconnaissance flights. The total ground force at the start was a few hundred Western soldiers, not a few hundred thousand.

The Campaign of October–December 2001

The bombs began to fall at 8:57 pm Kabul time on 7 October 2001 — less than four weeks after 9/11. Cruise missiles and B-1, B-2 and B-52 bombers struck Taliban airfields, training camps and air-defence radars. For three weeks the Taliban front lines held remarkably firm; the Northern Alliance, advised by US Special Forces calling in air strikes, made slow gains. Then the line collapsed. The northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif fell on 9 November, Kabul on 13 November, Jalalabad two days later. Cornered Taliban and al-Qaeda fighters retreated south to Kandahar and to the cave complexes of Tora Bora.

In early December 2001, US air power and Afghan militias closed in on Tora Bora, where bin Laden had taken refuge. American commanders later admitted they had relied on Afghan proxies rather than committing US troops to seal the mountain passes. Bin Laden and several hundred fighters slipped over the border into Pakistan’s tribal areas. A 2009 US Senate Foreign Relations Committee report called the failure to commit ground troops at Tora Bora the moment Washington missed its best chance to capture or kill bin Laden, an opportunity that would not recur until the Abbottabad raid in 2011.

Why the Regime Collapsed So Fast

Kandahar fell on 7 December 2001. The Taliban regime had lasted barely two months under Western pressure. Three factors explain the speed of the collapse. First, the Taliban’s air force and air defences were destroyed within ten days, removing any defence against precision bombing. Second, US special forces and CIA officers paid local commanders enormous sums in cash to switch sides; whole districts changed hands without a fight. Third, the Northern Alliance had spent five years preparing for this moment and pushed forward with conviction once Western air power broke the Taliban front line. The Western footprint was deliberately small — the model would later be called ‘the Afghan model’ — and it gave the United States a quick military victory that it could not later translate into political stability.

Key Fact

The Taliban regime fell in just 63 days from the opening air strikes on 7 October 2001 to the fall of Kandahar on 7 December. The victory was won mostly by Afghan ground troops backed by American and British air power, not by massed Western forces — with major consequences for what came next.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Bush’s ‘war on terror’ doctrine combined ultimatum (deliver al-Qaeda or share their fate), pre-emption (strike before being attacked) and the ‘axis of evil’ framing of Iraq, Iran and North Korea.
  • Operation Enduring Freedom from 7 October 2001 used US/UK air power, CIA Special Activities teams and Northern Alliance ground troops; NATO invoked Article 5 for the first time in its history.
  • The Taliban regime fell in 63 days, but bin Laden escaped at Tora Bora — a missed opportunity that shaped the next decade of the war.

Source A: Extract from President George W. Bush’s address to a joint session of Congress, 20 September 2001.
‘Tonight, the United States of America makes the following demands on the Taliban: deliver to United States authorities all the leaders of al-Qaeda who hide in your land. Close every terrorist training camp in Afghanistan. The Taliban must act, and act immediately. They will hand over the terrorists, or they will share in their fate. Every nation in every region now has a decision to make. Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists.’

What can be learned from Source A about Bush’s aims after the 11 September attacks?

Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise quotation from the source.
Secure: Two inferences with at least one quotation.
Developing: One inference with limited evidence.
Emerging: Paraphrase without inference.

Indicative content:
• The phrase ‘or they will share in their fate’ suggests Bush regarded the Taliban regime itself as a legitimate military target, not just al-Qaeda; this is a doctrine of state responsibility for harbouring terrorists.
• The list of demands — deliver leaders, close every camp — suggests Bush was framing public, unconditional terms that the Taliban could not accept without losing power.
• The line ‘either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists’ implies a global doctrine: third states would be judged by their attitude to the United States, leaving little neutral ground.
• The address’s tone, given to Congress nine days after 9/11, suggests Bush was deliberately raising the political cost of any later restraint.

practice_questions.text:
Source B: Photograph from Bagram airbase, mid-November 2001. The image shows two US Special Forces soldiers on horseback alongside Northern Alliance fighters in turbans and woollen pakol caps. A B-52 contrail crosses the sky above them. Western press captioned the image ‘The 21st-Century Cavalry’.

What can be learned from Source B about how the United States fought the 2001 campaign in Afghanistan?

Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise detail of the source (horsemen, B-52 contrail, Northern Alliance fighters, Western caption).

• The B-52 contrail above suggests how the war was actually being won — precision air power directed by small ground teams — rather than by horseback charges.
• The Western press caption ‘The 21st-Century Cavalry’ suggests how American media framed the campaign as fast, romantic and heroic, helping to sustain domestic political support in the early phase.
• The image’s composition, showing American and Afghan fighters together, suggests an effort to portray the campaign as a partnership rather than a Western occupation.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Taliban regime in Afghanistan was overthrown between 7 October and 7 December 2001.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (opening air strikes 7 October, fall of Mazar 9 November, Kabul 13 November, Tora Bora December, fall of Kandahar 7 December); arrives at the destruction of the regime through clear causation.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 7 October 2001: US/UK air strikes opened against Taliban command and air-defence sites; Taliban air defences collapsed within days.
• Late October: US Special Forces deployed alongside Northern Alliance ground commanders, calling in air strikes onto Taliban front lines.
• 9 November: Mazar-i-Sharif fell, opening the road north and east; CIA cash payments encouraged local commanders to switch sides.

• Late November: cornered Taliban and al-Qaeda fighters retreated to Tora Bora and Kandahar.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how Tony Blair’s government committed Britain to the 2001 Afghanistan campaign.

Mastering: Analytical chain linking three or more events with precise detail (‘shoulder to shoulder’ speech 11 September, Article 5 invocation 12 September, Cabinet decisions, opening cruise-missile strikes from Royal Navy submarines, SAS deployment); reaches the British role in the fall of Kabul through clear causation.

• 12 September: NATO invoked Article 5 for the first time, giving Blair a multilateral framework for British action.
• Mid-September: emergency Cabinet meetings authorised contingency planning by the Ministry of Defence.

practice_questions.text:
‘The speed of the Taliban’s collapse in 2001 was due mainly to American air power.’
Using the sources and your knowledge, explore how far you accept this view.

Source A: Extract from Bush’s 20 September 2001 address to Congress (described above).
Source B: Photograph of US Special Forces with Northern Alliance fighters at Bagram, November 2001 (described above).
Source C: Extract from a December 2001 Reuters dispatch from Mazar-i-Sharif. ‘General Dostum’s men entered the city in pickup trucks. The bombing had done the rest. Of the Taliban governor’s headquarters there was little left but rubble; the streets were lined with men celebrating. ‘The Americans are good friends,’ said one fighter, holding up a fistful of US dollars.’
