Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement weighing air power against ground proxies, CIA cash, political miscalculation by the Taliban, and Northern Alliance preparation; explicit use of all three sources and contextual knowledge of provenance.
Secure: Both views supported by source content and own knowledge; clear judgement.
Developing: One side fully developed; limited use of sources.
Emerging: Description of sources without sustained argument.

Indicative content:
• In support: Source B’s B-52 contrail and Source C’s description of Mazar (‘the bombing had done the rest’) show that conventional Taliban defences could not survive precision air strikes; opening strikes from 7 October destroyed the air force and command structure within ten days.
• Against: Source B also shows ground proxies were essential to convert air power into territory; without the Northern Alliance, air strikes would have produced no occupation. Source C’s detail of US dollars suggests CIA cash was buying loyalty as decisively as bombs.
• Source A’s ultimatum is also a cause — by demanding terms the Taliban could not accept, Bush ensured a war the regime was politically isolated to fight.
• Provenance: Source C is a Reuters wire dispatch close to events, with the limits of an early front-line account; Source B is a Western press image curated to celebrate the campaign.
• Judgement: air power was the immediate enabler, but the speed of collapse depended on the combination — air strikes, ground proxies, cash and political shock; on its own air power had not removed the Taliban in three weeks of bombing before mid-November.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Battle of Tora Bora in the 2001 Afghanistan campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and in consequence; precise factual detail (December 2001 location, US reliance on Afghan militias, bin Laden’s escape into Pakistan, 2009 Senate report, link to long war).
Secure: Significance argued on at least two grounds with detail.
Developing: Importance described rather than explained.
Emerging: Generic comments.

Indicative content:
• Tora Bora was the moment when American military success in Afghanistan failed to translate into the capture of al-Qaeda’s leadership — the immediate aim of the campaign.
• The decision to use Afghan militias rather than commit US ground troops to seal the mountain passes meant bin Laden and several hundred fighters escaped into Pakistan’s tribal areas.
• A 2009 US Senate Foreign Relations Committee report concluded that the failure was the missed opportunity to end al-Qaeda’s leadership in 2001; bin Laden remained at large until the 2011 Abbottabad raid.
• Tora Bora exposed the limits of the ‘light footprint’ Afghan model that had brought such rapid success in October and November.
• In consequence, al-Qaeda’s survival in Pakistan’s tribal areas underwrote the long counter-insurgency that Western forces would still be fighting in Helmand and Kandahar a decade later.

lessons.title: Karzai, Bonn and the Long Resurgence of the Taliban

before.content_html:
From Kandahar to Bonn

By the time Kandahar fell on 7 December 2001, foreign diplomats and Afghan factions were already gathered in a hotel above the Rhine in Bonn, Germany. The United Nations had brought four delegations together: the Northern Alliance, two exile groups based in Rome and Cyprus, and a Pashtun delegation from Peshawar. The Taliban were excluded. The British diplomat Lakhdar Brahimi, working for the UN, chaired the talks. Their job was to agree what came next: a transitional administration, a roadmap to a constitution and elections, and an international force to keep order in Kabul.

Key Fact

The December 2001 Bonn Conference brought four Afghan delegations together but excluded the Taliban. It chose Hamid Karzai as interim leader, set out a roadmap to a Loya Jirga and elections, and authorised the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) to keep order in Kabul.

Hamid Karzai and the Bonn Agreement

The Bonn delegates needed a Pashtun figure to balance the Tajik and Uzbek dominance of the Northern Alliance. They chose Hamid Karzai, an English-speaking Popalzai tribal leader from Kandahar whose father had been assassinated by the Taliban in 1999. The Bonn Agreement, signed on 5 December 2001, made him chairman of an Afghan Interim Administration for six months. While the talks were ending, Karzai was on the ground in Uruzgan province nearly killed by an American air strike that hit the wrong target. He was inaugurated in Kabul on 22 December.

ISAF and the Light Western Footprint

UN Security Council Resolution 1386, passed on 20 December 2001, authorised the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) to maintain security in Kabul and its surrounding area. The early ISAF was deliberately small: around 4,500 troops drawn from 18 countries, led at first by Britain and then by Turkey. Outside Kabul, security was left to regional warlords whom the United States and Britain had bought as allies during the campaign — Abdul Rashid Dostum in the north, Ismail Khan in Herat, Gul Agha Sherzai in Kandahar. Donald Rumsfeld, the US Defense Secretary, refused requests from Karzai and Brahimi to expand ISAF outside Kabul. The light footprint was a deliberate choice and it shaped everything that followed.

Bonn had promised an emergency Loya Jirga — a Pashto term meaning ‘grand assembly’ — to confirm a transitional government. It met in Kabul in June 2002 and elected Karzai head of state. A constitutional Loya Jirga in December 2003 produced a new constitution in January 2004: an Islamic republic with a strong elected president, a national assembly and equal rights for women on paper. In October 2004 Karzai was elected president with 55% of the vote in the country’s first direct presidential election. The procedural milestones of the Bonn process were largely met. The political reality on the ground was less reassuring.

The Problems Karzai Faced

Karzai inherited four overlapping problems. The first was warlordism: regional commanders ran their provinces as personal fiefdoms, kept their militias, taxed the population and, in some cases, ran the police. The second was the opium economy. Afghanistan had produced about 185 tonnes of opium in 2001 under Taliban suppression; by 2007 it was producing 8,200 tonnes — over 90% of the world’s heroin supply — and the trade funded both warlords and a returning insurgency. The third was corruption. Police salaries went unpaid for months at a time, ministers awarded contracts to relatives and the Kabul Bank scandal of 2010 would later expose nearly $1 billion missing. The fourth was Karzai’s own legitimacy: he was widely nicknamed ‘the Mayor of Kabul’, partly because of how little authority he had outside the capital and partly because his personal security depended on a US contractor team.

The Resurgence of the Taliban

The Taliban had fled in late 2001 rather than fight to the death. Many crossed into Pakistan’s tribal areas, where ISI sympathisers and a sympathetic Pashtun population sheltered them. From 2002 they began rebuilding. By 2005 a low-level insurgency was reaching across southern and eastern Afghanistan. NATO took over command of ISAF from August 2003, expanded it nationwide from 2006, and committed itself to the south — British forces deployed to Helmand Province from May 2006 expecting a peacekeeping role and finding themselves in some of the heaviest fighting British troops had seen since the Falklands.

Three factors fed the resurgence. First, the Taliban’s sanctuary in Pakistan’s tribal areas was never closed; ISI elements continued quiet support, and US drone strikes were politically constrained until 2008. Second, the Karzai government’s failure to deliver justice, jobs or honest policing in southern districts left openings the Taliban filled with shadow courts that paid villagers more reliably than the state. Third, opium money paid for fighters, weapons and motorcycles. Western forces fought campaign after campaign — Operation Mountain Thrust 2006, Operation Medusa, the years of bloody fighting in Sangin from 2006 — without ever shutting down the supply of recruits coming north out of Pakistan.

Key Fact

By 2006 the Taliban had recovered enough to launch a sustained insurgency in southern and eastern Afghanistan. Helmand opium funded fighters; Pakistan’s tribal areas housed their leadership; the Karzai government’s weakness gave them political openings. The 2001 victory had not held.
before.exam_tip_html: A 12-mark Source Evaluation question (sometimes shorter) on the problems faced by Karzai’s government will give you two sources of different types — perhaps a UN report and a journalist’s account — and ask how useful they are. Address content (what each source tells you), provenance (who wrote it, when, why) and your contextual knowledge (what you can verify or qualify). The top-band response weighs all three for both sources, never just two; explicitly compare them and reach an overall judgement on relative usefulness.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Extract from a UN Office on Drugs and Crime country report on Afghan opium production, published 2007.
‘In 2001 Afghan opium poppy cultivation stood at around 8,000 hectares following the Taliban ban; by 2007 it has reached 193,000 hectares. Production is concentrated in Helmand province, where the insurgency has secured the cooperation of farmers and traders. The opium economy now exceeds the legal export earnings of the Afghan state.’

What can be learned from Source A about the problems faced by Karzai’s government?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise figure or phrase from the source.
Secure: Two inferences with at least one supporting detail.
Developing: One inference; some detail.
Emerging: Description without inference.

Indicative content:
• The 24-fold increase in cultivation suggests Karzai’s government had no effective drug-control policy in the south — a policy area in which the Taliban regime had demonstrably succeeded.
• The phrase ‘the insurgency has secured the cooperation of farmers’ suggests opium was binding villagers to the Taliban, not the government, in the very provinces where Karzai needed legitimacy.
• That the opium economy ‘exceeds legal export earnings’ suggests the formal Afghan economy was being dwarfed by an illegal one Karzai could not tax or regulate.
• The concentration in Helmand suggests the insurgency had a stable revenue base in the British zone of operations — a point of obvious concern to a UN agency.

practice_questions.text:
Source B: Extract from a 2006 BBC report on the British deployment to Helmand province.
‘The Defence Secretary said it would be a peacekeeping mission and we hoped not to fire a shot. Six weeks in, our company has been in firefights almost every day. We are at platoon houses scattered across the province, dug in behind sandbags, fighting Taliban units that nobody told us would still be here.’

What can be learned from Source B about the resurgence of the Taliban by 2006?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise quotation from the source.
Secure: Two inferences with at least one quotation.
Developing: One inference with limited evidence.
Emerging: Paraphrase without inference.

Indicative content:
• The phrase ‘we hoped not to fire a shot’ suggests British political leaders had badly misread the security situation in southern Afghanistan in 2006.
• The line ‘Taliban units that nobody told us would still be here’ suggests intelligence and policy briefings underestimated the regrowth of the movement; the resurgence had outpaced the government’s assessment of it.
• The reference to ‘platoon houses scattered across the province’ suggests British forces were spread thinly, holding ground rather than dominating it — a sign of how serious the resurgence already was.
• The contrast between ‘peacekeeping’ rhetoric and ‘firefights almost every day’ suggests British forces faced organised insurgent units, not isolated terrorists, by mid-2006.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how Hamid Karzai’s government was established between November 2001 and October 2004.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Bonn conference December 2001, ISAF authorisation, emergency Loya Jirga 2002, constitutional Loya Jirga December 2003, January 2004 constitution, October 2004 election); reaches the elected presidency through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• November 2001: with Kandahar still falling, the UN convened four Afghan delegations in Bonn under Lakhdar Brahimi.
• 5 December 2001: the Bonn Agreement made Karzai chairman of an Afghan Interim Administration; he was inaugurated in Kabul on 22 December.
• 20 December 2001: UN Security Council Resolution 1386 authorised ISAF to maintain security in Kabul.
• June 2002: an emergency Loya Jirga elected Karzai head of state for the transitional period.
• December 2003: a constitutional Loya Jirga drafted the new constitution.
• January 2004: the constitution was promulgated, declaring Afghanistan an Islamic republic with elected institutions.
• October 2004: Karzai was elected president with 55% of the vote in the country’s first direct presidential election.
• The Bonn roadmap had been delivered procedurally even as the country’s underlying problems went unsolved.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Taliban regrouped and returned to fighting between 2002 and 2006.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical chain linking three or more events with precise detail (flight to Pakistan tribal areas, ISI sympathies, opium revenue, low-level violence 2002–05, NATO expansion 2006, Helmand deployment); reaches the full insurgency through clear causation.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causation.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• Late 2001–early 2002: Taliban and al-Qaeda fighters fled south and east into Pakistan’s tribal areas where parts of the ISI continued to give quiet support.
• 2002–04: small Taliban units began re-entering Afghanistan to attack district centres and government officials.
• By 2005 the opium harvest in Helmand was funding fighters, weapons and motorcycles; shadow courts began operating in Pashtun villages.
• August 2003: NATO took over ISAF, but the force was still concentrated in Kabul.
• 2006: NATO expanded ISAF nationwide; British forces deployed to Helmand from May 2006 expecting peacekeeping and meeting heavy combat.
• By the end of 2006 a full insurgency was under way across the south and east, with Operation Mountain Thrust and Operation Medusa testing the new NATO posture.

practice_questions.text:
‘The light Western footprint after 2001 was the most important reason the Karzai government failed to control Afghanistan.’
Using the sources and your knowledge, explore how far you accept this view.

Source A: 2007 UN Office on Drugs and Crime extract on Helmand opium (described above).
Source B: 2006 BBC report from Helmand on British deployment (described above).
Source C: Memoir extract by Lakhdar Brahimi, the UN’s Bonn chairman, written in 2010. ‘We pleaded with Washington to expand ISAF beyond Kabul. Rumsfeld refused. The warlords kept their militias. The drugs went unaddressed. We had built a constitution but not a state. The window was real, and we lost it.’
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement weighing the ‘light footprint’ against alternative factors (warlordism, opium, Pakistan sanctuary, corruption); explicit use of all three sources and their provenance.
Secure: Both views supported by source content and own knowledge; clear judgement.
Developing: One side fully developed; limited use of sources.
Emerging: Description of sources without sustained argument.

Indicative content:
• In support: Source C is unusually direct — the UN chairman of the Bonn process himself attributes failure to Washington’s refusal to expand ISAF outside Kabul. Source B’s account of platoon houses scattered across Helmand shows what the eventual NATO redeployment looked like once the gap had been allowed to open.
• Against: Source A points to the opium economy as a structural problem that no troop level could have solved on its own without alternative livelihoods, alternative judiciary and serious police reform. The Pakistan sanctuary — not addressed by any of the sources directly — was beyond the reach of any Western footprint inside Afghanistan.
• Provenance: Source C is a retrospective memoir with all the advantages and limits of hindsight; Source A is an institutional UN report with disciplinary expertise; Source B is a contemporary war-zone dispatch.
• Judgement: the light footprint was the decision that allowed warlordism, the opium economy and the Pakistan sanctuary to consolidate; it was therefore the enabling cause that made the others unmanageable. But it is too narrow to call it the ‘most important reason’ alone — the structural problems would have been hard to fix even with more troops, especially without a serious Pakistan policy.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the December 2001 Bonn Conference for the future of Afghanistan.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and in consequence; precise factual detail (UN-chaired, four delegations, Taliban excluded, Karzai chosen, Loya Jirga roadmap, ISAF authorised, light footprint).
Secure: Significance argued on at least two grounds with detail.
Developing: Importance described rather than explained.
Emerging: Generic comments.

Indicative content:
• Bonn was the moment Afghan factions agreed a transitional government in days rather than months, giving Karzai the legitimacy to take office before the war was fully over.
• The choice to exclude the Taliban turned a defeated insurgency into a permanent opposition; later attempts to negotiate would always have to overcome that initial decision.
• The Bonn roadmap to a Loya Jirga and a constitution shaped Afghan politics for the next decade and produced the January 2004 constitution.
• ISAF’s authorisation under UN Resolution 1386 created the multilateral framework that would eventually carry NATO across the country, but its initial limit to Kabul fixed the ‘light footprint’ that allowed warlordism to consolidate.
• In consequence Bonn shaped both the achievements (constitution, elections, Karzai’s presidency) and the failures (warlords, opium, Taliban resurgence) of the years that followed.

lessons.title: Saddam, WMD and the Road to the 2003 Invasion

before.content_html:
Saddam in the Twelve Years After Desert Storm

Between the 1991 ceasefire and the 2003 invasion, Saddam Hussein remained in power but operated under conditions no other state faced. UN sanctions, two coalition no-fly zones and an inspections regime were designed to contain his regime without removing it. Inside Iraq, repression deepened. The 1988 chemical-weapon attack on Halabja, in which roughly 5,000 Kurds were killed by Iraqi air-force sarin and mustard-gas bombs, was already on the international record. After 1991 Saddam crushed the Shia uprising in the south — mass graves uncovered after 2003 confirmed killings in the tens of thousands — and drained the southern marshes to displace the Marsh Arabs from a territory the regime could no longer police. The 1995 oil-for-food programme, intended to soften the impact of sanctions on civilians, was siphoned by the regime to reward loyalists.

Key Fact

Saddam’s record on which the 2003 invasion was justified was real: the 1988 Halabja chemical attack killed around 5,000 Kurds; the post-1991 suppression of the Shia uprising killed tens of thousands. UN Resolution 1441, passed unanimously in November 2002, gave him ‘a final opportunity to comply’ with disarmament obligations dating back to 1991.

Religious Divisions and the Question of Iraq

Iraq is a Shia-majority country — around 60% of the population — ruled until 2003 by a Sunni Arab elite drawn from Saddam’s home region around Tikrit. The Kurdish north (mostly Sunni but ethnically distinct) had operated as a semi-autonomous region under no-fly-zone protection since 1991. These divisions mattered for two reasons. They had shaped the brutality of the 1991 Shia and Kurdish uprisings, and they would shape the insurgency that followed the 2003 invasion. The Bush administration’s plans for post-Saddam Iraq assumed that the Shia majority and the Kurds would welcome liberation; they did. The plans paid less attention to what would happen to the displaced Sunni minority once the army and the Ba’ath party were dissolved.

After 9/11: Linking Saddam to al-Qaeda

From late 2001, senior figures in the Bush administration argued that Saddam might supply weapons of mass destruction to terrorist groups. Vice-President Dick Cheney repeatedly suggested that the lead 9/11 hijacker had met an Iraqi intelligence officer in Prague. The 9/11 Commission Report (2004) and the Senate Intelligence Committee report (2006) both concluded there was no operational link between Saddam and al-Qaeda. The two were ideologically opposed: Saddam ran a secular Ba’athist state, bin Laden a Sunni jihadist movement that considered Saddam’s regime apostate. Despite this, polling in 2003 showed around 70% of Americans believed Saddam was personally involved in 9/11. The link was a political construction, not an established fact.

In September 2002 Tony Blair’s government published ‘Iraq’s Weapons of Mass Destruction: The Assessment of the British Government’, known popularly as the September Dossier. It carried a foreword by Blair claiming Saddam’s WMD capability was ‘active, detailed and growing’. Most controversially, the document repeated four times an intelligence claim that Iraqi forces could deploy chemical or biological weapons within 45 minutes of an order. The Hutton Inquiry (2004) and the Chilcot Inquiry (2016) both judged the dossier had been presented with ‘a certainty that was not justified’. Chilcot wrote that No. 10 had taken ‘the most optimistic top line of every issue and played down the problems and the caveats and the warnings’.

UNMOVIC, Blix and the Inspectors

UN Resolution 1441, passed unanimously by the Security Council on 8 November 2002, ordered Iraq to readmit weapons inspectors. The team that returned was led by the Swedish diplomat Hans Blix for the United Nations Monitoring, Verification and Inspection Commission (UNMOVIC), with the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Mohamed ElBaradei in charge of the nuclear file. Between November 2002 and March 2003 they conducted around 700 inspections at over 500 sites. Blix told the Security Council on 27 January 2003 that Iraq’s 12,000-page declaration was incomplete but that cooperation had improved; on 7 March he reported ‘tangible’ though gradual progress and asked for more time. ElBaradei told the same session that documents on Iraqi nuclear procurement — presented to the Council by US Secretary of State Colin Powell on 5 February — had been forged. The inspectors had not found WMD. They had not concluded that none existed. The Bush administration treated the absence of certainty as proof of concealment.

February 2003 and the Largest Anti-War Protests in History

On 15 February 2003, an estimated 6–10 million people took part in coordinated demonstrations across more than 600 cities, against the looming invasion. Around 1 million marched in London — the largest demonstration in British history at that time. The protests were notable for their breadth: trade unions, faith leaders, academics, anti-war veterans of the 1991 Gulf War and ordinary civilians who had not previously demonstrated. They did not change government policy. The British House of Commons voted in favour of military action on 18 March 2003 by 412 to 149, although 139 Labour MPs rebelled against their own Prime Minister. Failing to secure a second UN resolution explicitly authorising war — France made clear it would veto — the United States and the United Kingdom assembled what Washington called a ‘coalition of the willing’ outside the UN framework.

A common student error is to treat the WMD intelligence as either obviously correct or a deliberate lie. The Hutton Report (2004) and the Chilcot Report (2016) showed it was contested and selectively presented. Inspectors said no active programmes had been verified; intelligence agencies said small quantities probably existed; political leaders said the threat was clear, urgent and growing. The Iraq Survey Group, after the invasion, concluded that Iraq had ended its WMD programmes in the 1990s but kept the option of restarting them — the picture closest to what Blix had been describing all along.

Key Fact

The road to war ran through three formal moments and one non-event. UN Resolution 1441 (8 November 2002) gave Iraq a final opportunity to disarm. Hans Blix’s reports of January and March 2003 found no WMD but limited cooperation. The 15 February 2003 global protests were the largest in history. The non-event was the second UN resolution explicitly authorising force, which the United States and United Kingdom never secured.
before.exam_tip_html: A 16-mark Source-Based Essay on whether the 2003 invasion was justified will give you two or three sources of different dates — a 2002 dossier, an inspector’s January 2003 report, a 2016 inquiry. Treat the dates as evidence in their own right: a contemporary case-making document is not the same as a retrospective inquiry. Reach a substantiated overall judgement that weighs both sides and integrates source content, provenance and your own contextual knowledge. Avoid first-person narrative and avoid quoting wholesale from the sources; paraphrase and embed.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Statement to the United Nations Security Council by Hans Blix, Executive Chairman of UNMOVIC, on 27 January 2003.
‘Iraq appears not to have come to a genuine acceptance — not even today — of the disarmament that was demanded of it… However, the inspections have not found such weapons.’
Source B: Foreword by the Prime Minister Tony Blair to the British government dossier ‘Iraq’s Weapons of Mass Destruction’, September 2002.
‘What I believe the assessed intelligence has established beyond doubt is that Saddam has continued to produce chemical and biological weapons, that he continues in his efforts to develop nuclear weapons, and that he has been able to extend the range of his ballistic missile programme.’
Source C: Extract from the Iraq Inquiry Report (Chilcot Report), published in July 2016.
‘The judgements about the severity of the threat posed by Iraq’s weapons of mass destruction… were presented with a certainty that was not justified.’

‘The decision to invade Iraq in 2003 was justified by the available evidence.’
Using the sources and your knowledge, explore how far you accept this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement weighing the sources against each other, integrating provenance (date, author, audience) and own contextual knowledge to reach a clear conclusion.
Secure: Both views supported by source content and own knowledge with a clear judgement.
Developing: One side fully developed; limited use of sources.
Emerging: Description of sources without sustained argument.

Indicative content:
• In support: Source B reflects the official British public assessment in September 2002 — chemical and biological production, missile-range extension, nuclear-programme intent. Saddam’s record at Halabja and against the Shia in 1991 made the threat plausible. UN Resolution 1441 was passed unanimously, including by France and Russia, accepting the disarmament obligation existed.
• Against: Source A’s January 2003 statement from Blix — issued by an inspector with direct access — found no WMD. Source C’s 2016 Chilcot judgement that the case was presented with ‘a certainty that was not justified’ is the official British verdict on the dossier in Source B. ElBaradei reported in March 2003 that nuclear documents were forged. The largest anti-war protests in history (15 February 2003) suggest the public case was not credibly made.
• Provenance and reliability: Source B is a case-making document by a politician seeking to justify war; Source A is a working inspector’s update with operational evidence; Source C is an inquiry with hindsight and authority. Date and audience matter: 2016 hindsight is not 2002 advocacy.
• Judgement: the available evidence at the time was contested rather than conclusive; the Hutton and Chilcot inquiries judged the public presentation of it overstated. The invasion was a political decision the contested evidence could not, by itself, justify.

practice_questions.text:
Source D: Photograph of around one million people on Hyde Park Corner, central London, on 15 February 2003, gathered for the Stop the War Coalition rally on the eve of the Iraq War. Banners read ‘Not in My Name’ and ‘Listen to the Inspectors’.

What can be learned from Source D about British public opinion on the eve of the Iraq War?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise detail of the source.
Secure: Two inferences with at least one detail.
Developing: One inference with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the photograph without inference.

Indicative content:
• The scale of the crowd — described as around one million on Hyde Park Corner alone — implies that opposition to the war was not confined to the political left or to traditional protest groups; it was a mainstream public position.
• The slogan ‘Listen to the Inspectors’ implies that the protesters did not reject the disarmament process itself, but believed the UN inspections under Blix should be allowed to run their course before military action was authorised.
• ‘Not in My Name’ implies a sense of personal political identity being tied to opposition: protesters are distinguishing themselves from a government acting on their behalf rather than rejecting government authority altogether.
• The choice of Hyde Park as a venue, on a single coordinated day with rallies in 600 cities worldwide, suggests a globally networked protest movement using the internet and mass media — features absent in earlier anti-war movements.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how UN-led diplomacy on Iraq developed between November 2002 and March 2003.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more turning points (Resolution 1441 8 November 2002; Blix 27 January 2003; Powell 5 February; ElBaradei March 2003; failure of second resolution mid-March) as a chain of cause and consequence.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; some links missing.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 8 November 2002: UN Resolution 1441 passed unanimously, giving Iraq ‘a final opportunity to comply’ and reactivating UNMOVIC under Blix.
• November–December 2002: inspectors return; Iraq submits a 12,000-page declaration that the US says is incomplete.
• 27 January 2003: Blix reports limited cooperation but no WMD found; the language is harder than US officials hoped for.
• 5 February 2003: Colin Powell presents intelligence to the Security Council; key documents are later shown by ElBaradei to be forged.
• 7 March 2003: Blix asks for more time, reporting tangible progress; France and Russia indicate they will not support a second resolution authorising force.
• Mid-March 2003: the US and UK abandon the second-resolution effort; the invasion is launched on 20 March.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of UN Security Council Resolution 1441 in the months between November 2002 and March 2003.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over the period; precise factual detail (unanimous passage 8 November 2002, return of UNMOVIC, Iraqi 12,000-page declaration, Blix and ElBaradei reports, second-resolution failure).
Secure: Two clear significances with development.
Developing: One developed and one undeveloped point.
Emerging: Description with limited reference to significance.

Indicative content:
• At the time, the unanimous passage — including Russia, France and China — re-established that the Security Council still treated Iraqi disarmament as a binding obligation, and brought UNMOVIC inspectors back into the country after a four-year absence.
• It established the procedural framework on which Blix and ElBaradei reported between January and March 2003, including the 12,000-page Iraqi declaration and the 700 inspections at over 500 sites.
• Significance over time: the absence of a second resolution explicitly authorising force exposed the legal weakness of the 2003 invasion and became a central charge in the Chilcot Inquiry’s 2016 verdict.
• It also marked the last moment when the major powers operated through the Council on Iraq; the bypassing of the UN in March 2003 reshaped the politics of intervention for a decade.

practice_questions.text: Explain a development in the public case for war presented by the British government between September 2002 and February 2003.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Coherent account of change over the period with specific developments dated; analytical links between the dossier, the parliamentary debate and the protests.
Secure: Two clear developments with some detail.
Developing: One developed point.
Emerging: Generalised account.

Indicative content:
• September 2002: the British government published the September Dossier with Blair’s foreword claiming the WMD capability was ‘active, detailed and growing’; the document made the ‘forty-five minute’ claim a centrepiece.
• Late 2002: the case shifted to UN-route diplomacy as Resolution 1441 was negotiated; ministers argued that British support for action was conditional on Iraqi non-cooperation.
• January–February 2003: as Blix reported limited progress but no WMD, the government published a second briefing — later dubbed the ‘dodgy dossier’ — partly drawn from a postgraduate thesis available online.
• February 2003: with around one million marching in London on 15 February, ministers argued that the UN process had been exhausted; the language shifted from disarmament to regime change as the route to compliance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the international response to Iraq in 2002–03 was different from the international response to Iraq in 1990–91.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear and supported differences, each rooted in concrete examples from this lesson and the wider unit.
Secure: Two differences with at least one specific example.
Developing: One developed difference; one undeveloped.
Emerging: General comments without concrete examples.

Indicative content:
• Different — in 1990 the UN Security Council unanimously authorised the use of force through Resolution 678; in 2003 the US and UK failed to secure a second resolution and assembled a coalition outside UN authorisation.
• Different — in 1990 the coalition included Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Syria as Arab partners; in 2003 most Arab states refused to host the operation, and Turkey’s parliament refused the use of its territory.
• Different — in 1991 European public opinion broadly accepted the war; in 2003 anti-war protests on 15 February brought 6–10 million onto the streets in over 600 cities.
• Different — in 1991 the casus belli was Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait, an act of aggression; in 2003 it was the contested claim of weapons of mass destruction.

before.content_html:
Invasion: 20 March to 9 April 2003

The invasion of Iraq, code-named Operation Iraqi Freedom, began at dawn on 20 March 2003 with cruise-missile strikes on a site in Baghdad where Saddam Hussein was wrongly believed to be sleeping. A US-led ground force of around 150,000 troops, with around 45,000 British troops in the south, crossed from Kuwait. Within three weeks the regime had collapsed. Baghdad fell on 9 April; television viewers watched US Marines and Iraqi civilians pull down a statue of Saddam in Firdos Square. On 1 May 2003, on the deck of the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, President George W. Bush declared major combat operations over under a banner reading ‘Mission Accomplished’. The phrase would haunt the rest of his presidency. The invasion had been swift; the war was about to begin.

Key Fact

The invasion ran from 20 March to 9 April 2003 — just twenty-one days from launch to the fall of Baghdad. President Bush’s 1 May 2003 ‘Mission Accomplished’ speech declared major combat operations over. The deadliest years of the war were still ahead.

The CPA, De-Ba’athification and the Disbanding of the Army

The American occupation authority, the Coalition Provisional Authority (CPA), was led by L. Paul Bremer. In May 2003 Bremer issued two orders. CPA Order 1 banned senior members of Saddam’s Ba’ath party from public-sector employment, a process called de-Ba’athification. CPA Order 2 dissolved the Iraqi army, sending around 400,000 soldiers home unpaid and armed. Together these decisions removed a generation of Sunni Arab teachers, doctors, civil servants and officers from public life and gave the future insurgency a ready-made pool of trained, humiliated recruits. Bremer believed the orders would prevent a return of the regime; later assessments — including the Chilcot Inquiry and the US Army’s own internal histories — judged them the most damaging Western decisions of the war.

Insurgency and Civil War, 2003–07

From late 2003, attacks on coalition forces escalated. The signature weapon was the improvised explosive device (IED), a roadside bomb often built from artillery shells looted from un-secured ammunition dumps. The insurgency drew in three overlapping groups: Sunni Ba’athist remnants, foreign jihadists who flowed in to fight Americans (organising under the banner of al-Qaeda in Iraq from 2004), and Shia militias linked to Iran. The bombing of the al-Askari Shia shrine in Samarra in February 2006 tipped Iraq into open sectarian civil war. Death squads from the Mahdi Army cleared Sunni neighbourhoods of Baghdad; al-Qaeda in Iraq cleared mixed neighbourhoods of Shia. Civilian deaths reached their peak in 2006–07; the Iraq Body Count project recorded more than 29,000 documented civilian dead in 2006 alone.

In April 2004 the American programme 60 Minutes II, and the New Yorker journalist Seymour Hersh, published photographs taken by US military police of detainee abuse at the Abu Ghraib prison west of Baghdad. The images — hooded men forced into sexual postures, a prisoner standing on a box with electrical wires attached — circulated in global media within hours. Eleven US soldiers were court-martialled. The senior commanders responsible for prison policy faced no criminal charges. The damage was strategic: the photographs gave al-Qaeda in Iraq the recruitment imagery it needed and stripped the United States of the human-rights framing that had been part of the case for war. Many historians treat April 2004 as the moment the war was politically lost, even as it had nearly five more years to run.

Saddam Captured, the Constitution and the Elections

On 13 December 2003, US forces found Saddam in a hidden cellar near Tikrit. He was tried by an Iraqi tribunal for the 1982 Dujail massacre of Shia villagers and hanged on 30 December 2006. The political timetable for replacing his regime ran in parallel. A transitional government took office in June 2004; a constitutional referendum was held in October 2005; the first full parliamentary elections under the new constitution took place in December 2005. Around 78% of voters turned out despite intimidation. The new prime minister, Nouri al-Maliki, took office in 2006 at the head of a Shia-dominated coalition. Sunni political participation was thin and would remain so. The institutions were in place; the legitimacy that should have come with them was not.

Global Blowback: Madrid, London and Beyond

The Iraq War damaged Western security elsewhere. On 11 March 2004 ten coordinated bombs on Madrid commuter trains killed 191 people; the attackers, inspired by al-Qaeda, cited Spanish participation in Iraq. On 7 July 2005 four British suicide bombers attacked the London Underground and a Number 30 bus, killing 52 people; the recordings the bombers left explicitly cited British policy in Iraq. The 2005 Bali bombings, the 2007 Glasgow airport attack, and a string of disrupted plots in Britain and Germany were all tied directly or rhetorically to the Iraq conflict. The argument that the invasion would reduce global terrorism failed its first test within a year of the fall of Baghdad.

In January 2007 Bush announced the deployment of an additional 30,000 US troops, mostly to Baghdad, under General David Petraeus. Known as the surge, the strategy paired more troops with a counter-insurgency doctrine focused on protecting civilians rather than hunting fighters. At the same time, Sunni tribes in Anbar province turned against the brutality of al-Qaeda in Iraq and accepted American support to fight back — the so-called Sunni Awakening. Civilian deaths fell sharply in 2008. The surge stabilised the war but did not resolve the political settlement; the underlying Sunni–Shia compromise was never reached.

Iraq by the End of the Bush Presidency

When Bush left office on 20 January 2009 Iraq was no longer at the peak of its civil war but had not been stabilised. The Status of Forces Agreement, signed by Bush and Maliki in November 2008, set the timetable for US combat troops to leave by 31 December 2011. Around 4,400 American servicemen had been killed in Iraq, and 179 British. Iraqi civilian deaths since 2003 stood, by Iraq Body Count’s documented count, at over 100,000, with broader estimates from epidemiological studies running into several hundred thousand. Around 4 million Iraqis had been displaced internally or as refugees. The Maliki government leaned increasingly on Iranian backing and excluded Sunni representation. Five years later, in 2014, the militants who had become Islamic State (ISIS) would seize Mosul. The Iraq War of 2003–09 cannot honestly be called over by 2009 — merely paused, with the conditions for the next round already in place.

Key Fact

By the end of the Bush presidency on 20 January 2009, the US-led invasion had cost around 4,400 American and 179 British military lives, more than 100,000 documented Iraqi civilian deaths, and the displacement of around four million Iraqis. The 2007 surge and Sunni Awakening had reduced violence, but the political settlement remained unfinished; ISIS would emerge from this unresolved war within five years.
before.exam_tip_html: For a 16-mark Source-Based Essay on whether Iraq was stable by the end of Bush’s presidency, the marker is looking for a substantiated overall judgement, not a list. Weigh the surge and Sunni Awakening (real reductions in violence by 2008, elections held, Saddam tried and executed) against the unresolved political settlement (sectarian power balance broken, four million displaced, the Status of Forces Agreement only setting a withdrawal timetable). Use invented but credible source provenance — for example, a 2008 RUSI briefing on the surge, a 2009 IISS retrospective on Iraqi displacement — and integrate it with your own knowledge.

glossary_terms.definition: The banner displayed during George W. Bush’s 1 May 2003 speech aboard USS Abraham Lincoln, declaring major combat operations in Iraq over; later seen as a symbol of premature victory claims.
The US-led occupation administration of Iraq, headed by L. Paul Bremer, between May 2003 and June 2004; responsible for de-Ba’athification and the disbanding of the Iraqi army.
The post-2003 process of removing senior Ba’ath party members from Iraqi public office and the army; widely judged to have fed the insurgency by leaving an alienated armed Sunni minority.
An improvised explosive device, often a roadside bomb made from artillery shells; the most lethal weapon used against coalition troops in Iraq.
An armed uprising against an occupying or governing force; in Iraq from 2003, a mix of Sunni Ba’athist, Sunni jihadist and Shia militia groups fought coalition troops and each other.
The 2007 deployment of an additional 30,000 US troops to Iraq under General David Petraeus, paired with a counter-insurgency strategy of population protection and engagement with Sunni tribes.
The 2006–07 movement of Sunni tribes in Anbar province against al-Qaeda in Iraq, supported with American weapons and money; central to the reduction in violence after the 2007 surge.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Briefing paper from a senior fellow of the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), London, dated November 2008, assessing the effects of the 2007 US surge in Iraq.
‘Civilian deaths in Baghdad have fallen by more than 70% since the surge’s peak deployment. Coalition combat deaths in October 2008 reached their lowest monthly figure since the invasion. The military trajectory is unmistakably better. Whether the political settlement will hold once US forces draw down is a separate question — and the answer is much less encouraging.’
Source B: Retrospective article in Survival (the journal of the International Institute for Strategic Studies, IISS), dated July 2009, by a former British Foreign Office Iraq analyst.
‘Iraq in January 2009 had elections, a constitution and an army of sorts. It also had four million displaced people, a sectarian government with no Sunni reach, and an officer class drawn from a single confession. The surge bought time. It did not buy a country.’

‘Iraq was stable by the end of George W. Bush’s presidency in January 2009.’
Using the sources and your knowledge, explore how far you accept this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement weighing source content, provenance and own contextual knowledge; reaches a clear conclusion that integrates military stabilisation against political fragility.
Secure: Both views supported by source content and own knowledge with a clear judgement.
Developing: One side fully developed; limited use of sources.
Emerging: Description of sources without sustained argument.

Indicative content:
• In support: Source A documents a more than 70% drop in Baghdad civilian deaths and the lowest monthly coalition death toll since the invasion; the Sunni Awakening had blunted al-Qaeda in Iraq; constitutional elections of December 2005 had produced a government; Saddam had been tried and executed in 2006; the Status of Forces Agreement of November 2008 set a credible withdrawal timetable.
• Against: Source B emphasises four million displaced, a sectarian government without Sunni reach, and an army drawn from a single confession; the underlying political settlement was unfinished; the surge’s gains were tactical, not structural.
• Provenance: Source A is a contemporary 2008 military assessment from a Western think tank close to coalition policy circles, useful for the immediate trajectory but optimistic in its short-term framing. Source B is a 2009 retrospective by a former Iraq analyst, with hindsight to view the country whole; both must be weighed.
• Own knowledge: violence had fallen but had not gone away — major bombings continued through 2009; Maliki’s exclusion of Sunni political participation set the conditions for ISIS’s emergence in 2014. Around 4,400 US troops, 179 UK troops and well over 100,000 Iraqi civilians had been killed.
• Judgement: Iraq was less violent in January 2009 than in 2006–07, but stability requires more than a fall in killings. By the test of an enduring political settlement, the country was not stable; the surge paused the war rather than ending it.

practice_questions.text:
Source C: Photograph published in international news media in May 2004 showing a hooded prisoner standing on a box with electrical wires attached to his hands and feet, taken by US military police at the Abu Ghraib prison, Iraq.

What can be learned from Source C about the conduct of the Iraq War in 2003–04?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise detail of the source.
Secure: Two inferences with at least one detail.
Developing: One inference with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the photograph without inference.

Indicative content:
• The fact that US military police took the photograph themselves implies abuse was treated by some service personnel as routine or even celebratory rather than concealed, suggesting weak supervision and a culture failure within the prison’s chain of command.
• The choice of imagery — hooded, posed, with mock electrical wires — implies that humiliation was a tool of interrogation rather than an unintended by-product, raising questions about the wider detention regime authorised in 2003–04.
• The publication of the image in international media in May 2004 implies that strategic damage was severe: the image circulated in al-Qaeda recruitment material and stripped the war of its human-rights framing.
• The fact that only enlisted soldiers, not their commanders, were court-martialled implies that institutional accountability was limited, deepening the legitimacy crisis the photograph caused.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the war in Iraq developed between the fall of Baghdad in April 2003 and the al-Askari shrine bombing in February 2006.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more turning points (Baghdad falls April 2003; CPA Orders 1 and 2 May 2003; ‘Mission Accomplished’ 1 May 2003; insurgency from late 2003; Saddam captured December 2003; Abu Ghraib April 2004; transitional government June 2004; elections December 2005; Samarra February 2006) as a chain of cause and consequence.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; some links missing.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 9 April 2003: Baghdad falls; the regime collapses but no plan exists for the transition.
• May 2003: CPA Orders 1 and 2 dissolve the Iraqi army and exclude Ba’ath-party members from public life, creating a pool of armed unemployed Sunni Arabs.
• Late 2003: insurgent attacks against coalition forces escalate; IEDs become the signature weapon.
• 13 December 2003: Saddam is captured near Tikrit but the war does not abate.
• April 2004: the publication of the Abu Ghraib photographs damages the war’s legitimacy at home and abroad.
• June 2004: a transitional government takes office; al-Qaeda in Iraq emerges as a foreign-fighter network.
• December 2005: parliamentary elections produce a Shia-dominated government with weak Sunni participation.
• 22 February 2006: the al-Askari Shia shrine in Samarra is bombed; sectarian civil war begins.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Coalition Provisional Authority’s May 2003 orders dissolving the Iraqi army and excluding Ba’ath-party members from public office.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and in consequence; precise factual detail (CPA Orders 1 and 2 by Bremer in May 2003, around 400,000 disbanded soldiers, exclusion of senior Ba’athists, fuel for the insurgency, Chilcot Inquiry verdict).
Secure: Two clear significances with development.
Developing: One developed and one undeveloped point.
Emerging: Description with limited reference to significance.

Indicative content:
• At the time, the orders were intended to prevent a return of Saddam’s regime and to demonstrate a clean break from Ba’athist rule; in practice they removed teachers, doctors and engineers from the public sector overnight.
• They created an armed and humiliated body of around 400,000 unpaid Sunni Arab soldiers who provided the future insurgency with trained recruits.
• Significance over time: the Chilcot Inquiry (2016), the US Army’s own internal histories, and most subsequent academic accounts judged these the most damaging Western policy decisions of the war.
• They locked in Sunni political alienation. By 2014 the same Sunni areas, deprived of state employment for over a decade, hosted ISIS — the long-term shadow cast by two CPA orders signed in May 2003.

practice_questions.text: Explain a development in violence and politics in Iraq between the 2007 surge and the end of the Bush presidency in January 2009.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Coherent account of change over the period with specific developments dated; analytical links between the surge, the Sunni Awakening and the unfinished political settlement.
Secure: Two clear developments with some detail.
Developing: One developed point.
Emerging: Generalised account.

Indicative content:
• January 2007: Bush announced an additional 30,000 US troops under Petraeus, with a counter-insurgency doctrine focused on population protection.
• Through 2007: Sunni tribes in Anbar province turned against al-Qaeda in Iraq and accepted American support — the Sunni Awakening — sharply reducing foreign-fighter access.
• 2008: civilian deaths in Baghdad fell by more than 70% from their peak; coalition combat deaths reached their lowest monthly figures since 2003.
• November 2008: the Status of Forces Agreement between Bush and Maliki set 31 December 2011 as the deadline for US combat troops to leave.
• January 2009: Bush left office with violence reduced but the political settlement unresolved; Maliki’s exclusion of Sunni political participation continued, leaving the structural conditions of the insurgency in place.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the conditions in Iraq in 2009 were similar or different to the conditions following the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear and supported similarities or differences, each rooted in concrete examples drawn from this lesson and the wider unit.
Secure: Two points with at least one specific example.
Developing: One developed point; one undeveloped.
Emerging: General comments without concrete examples.

Indicative content:
• Different — in 1991 Saddam was left in place and Western forces withdrew within months; in 2009 Saddam had been deposed and executed, but a US combat presence remained on a withdrawal timetable to 2011.
• Different — the 1991 ceasefire produced a stable if brutal Iraqi regime; by 2009 Iraq was a fragile sectarian state with four million displaced and a Maliki government dependent on Iranian backing.
• Similar — both end-states left major problems unresolved: in 1991 the survival of Saddam and the crushing of the Shia uprising; in 2009 the unresolved Sunni–Shia political settlement that ISIS would later exploit.
• Similar — in both cases American policymakers underestimated what would follow the formal end of combat operations, and in both cases the operational verdict (Kuwait liberated in 1991; the surge’s reduction in violence in 2008–09) outran the political verdict.
